articles.title: ‘Traumatizing’: hunger striker in ICE detention tells of force-feeding ordeal – and what made him crack
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Luis Alejandro Cora Perez says in messages to Guardian from inside Texas facility pain of force-feeding caused him to break strike

The text message that came from inside the…

blocks.text: The text message that came from inside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center was stark: “I have spent five days eating regular food. If I don’t eat it, they put the tube in me to feed me.”

A Cuban asylum seeker, Luis Alejandro Cora Perez, 32, said in messages to the Guardian this month that he was still weak and dizzy after three months without eating, but that he had broken his hunger strike because being force-fed was just too painful.
The Trump administration responded to requests for comment by denying it had force-fed Cora Perez. But the detainee sent more details – and his is far from an isolated case.
Cora Perez was one of two men on hunger striker at a Texas facility for whom ICE sought and received a federal judge’s permission to force-feed in recent weeks, a Guardian investigation found.

Cora Perez and the other man were locked up inside the Port Isabel service processing center, an ICE detention facility in south Texas, just a few miles from the US-Mexico border, on the coast near where Elon Musk’s SpaceX launches rockets. Cora Perez began a hunger strike in August to protest against his prolonged detention by federal immigration officials while his case plays out. At first he only drank water, then after three weeks, he says he began to drink one Ensure nutritional shake per day.
On 30 October, court records show ICE received permission to forcibly feed and hydrate him, and to restrain him while doing so.

The next day he says six guards at the center held him down, while medical staffers inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his throat, and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach – a process he called “traumatizing, both physically and psychologically”.

On 3 November, ICE then received permission from a federal judge to force-feed another hunger striker at Port Isabel, from Uzbekistan, federal court records show. DHS says the Uzbek man has not been subjected to the practice, however.

blocks.caption: The Port Isabel detention center in Los Fresnos, Texas. Photograph: Verónica G Cárdenas/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: On Wednesday night, after weeks of communications, Cora Perez was suddenly transferred to another detention center in Texas. His relative says neither of them were alerted to any plans to transfer him, or a reason for it.
DHS did not specify why Cora Perez was transferred, adding that ICE makes custody determinations on a “case-by-case” basis based on “various factors”.

The revelations come as ICE’s detention practices continue to come under fire amid allegations of mistreatment, and as an increasing number of sporadic hunger strikes have been breaking out in ICE facilities across the country.

The two men’s cases in Texas, revealed here for the first time, are some of the most recent instances of government lawyers seeking a federal judge’s permission, as required by ICE policy, and receiving the go-ahead to force-feed detained hunger strikers. The Guardian’s reporting is based on court records, interviews, dozens of messages exchanged and an interview conducted with Cora Perez via a facility phone. It further reveals how the Trump administration is increasingly obtaining such court orders to force-feed detained immigrants, a secretive practice widely condemned as torture by human rights organizations and medical ethics groups.

Detainees driven to hunger strike are typically using it as a last resort to protest against poor conditions and the Trump administration’s preference for arrest and prolonged detention while their civil immigration cases proceed through the system.

Cora Perez said detention center staff inserted the feeding tube and left it in his body, a not uncommon practice, according to experts, and introduced nutrition – first a “clear liquid”, followed by a “milky liquid”, he recalled – through the tube twice more that day, before he cracked and said he broke his hunger strike, citing what he called “horrific torture”. He began voluntarily drinking nutritional shakes the following day, he said.

“ICE does not hold back on anything, and they do anything they want, like we have seen, even killing their own US citizens,” he wrote to the Guardian, referring to the fatal shootings of Renee Good by an ICE officer and Alex Pretti by a border patrol officer in January of this year during Trump’s pivotal immigration crackdown on Minneapolis.

blocks.caption: Children look at posters honoring Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good, shot dead by federal agents in Minneapolis in January. Photograph: Tim Evans/Reuters

blocks.text: Detained hunger strikers subjected to involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding, have rarely spoken out about their cases or revealed their identities, much less while still detained. Cora Perez’s messages offer a rare glimpse at conditions inside a detention center’s restricted medical unit where hunger strikers and suicidal detainees are held.

“They just took [the Uzbek man] in an ambulance after [him] fainting in front of the medical lobby where they take our vitals, our weight and our temperature,” Cora said in an alarmed message last Monday morning.
The Uzbek man was returned the following day to the facility, Cora Perez said.
“I see him every day because I see him in the room in front of me, but they don’t let us talk to each other,” he added.

The Guardian independently confirmed the Uzbek’s man identity but is not publicly naming him, because efforts to contact him have been unsuccessful. The man arrived at the Mexico-US border in April 2022 and was released into the country while navigating his immigration case. He was arrested by border patrol officials in April of this year and placed in detention. The man does not appear to have any criminal record and DHS did not point to any criminal history.
In a statement, DHS said that after they received the court’s permission to force-feed the Uzbek man, he “has voluntarily taken in fluids and there has been NO force-feeding or forced hydration”.

Security operations at the sprawling Port Isabel facility in Los Fresnos, Texas are run by a private prison company, Akima Global Services, while healthcare is primarily handled by government workers.

blocks.caption: An examination area of the Port Isabel facility. Photograph: Verónica G Cárdenas/AFP via Getty Images

blocks.text: “ICE respects detainees’ rights to exercise self-expression and medical autonomy by refusing nourishment and medical care,” DHS said in a statement. “ICE Health Services Corps may provide involuntary medical treatment only to prevent imminent life-threatening harm or death. Medical staff may provide treatment only to medically stabilize the patient, bringing the detainee outside the imminent harm, incapacitation, or death.”

The US attorney’s office in the southern district of Texas, which represented ICE in its force-feeding request, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Virginia-headquartered Akima Global Services, and its parent company Nana Regional Corporation, based in Alaska, did not respond to a request for comment.

Force-feeding cases are shrouded in secrecy. After a detainee launches a hunger strike, ICE often sequesters them in medical isolation cells for monitoring, according to ICE’s detention standards. DHS said that ICE continues to offer hunger strikers three meals per day.

After a certain period of not eating, which varies per case, ICE will request a federal judge’s permission to force-feed the hunger striker. Many court records, and sometimes entire court dockets, are sealed and hidden from public view. In Cora Perez and the Uzbek man’s cases, like in others, they did not have any legal representation to challenge the force-feeding requests.

The Guardian found at least five instances in which ICE requested permission to force-feed hunger strikers in Port Isabel since January 2025. The federal judge who ruled on Cora Perez and the Uzbek man, Rolando Olvera, has similarly ordered in at least three other cases, records show. Olvera’s judicial assistant said the court had no comment for this article.

ICE is known to have requested permission to force-feed at least 21 detainees across the US since January 2025, the Guardian found, but the number is likely higher since an unknown number of records and dockets remain sealed, unsearchable and not feasible to locate. Most of the cases coinciding with the second Trump administration and tracked by the Guardian are in Texas and Florida, with others in Georgia, Arizona and Washington state. Under the Biden administration, ICE force-feeding requests were also made in Louisiana and California.

Amy Zeidan, an emergency medicine physician based in Atlanta and an expert on healthcare in immigration detention, said force-feeding hunger strikers can amount to “torture”, and lead to significant psychological distress. She also said it is a violation of medical ethics.

“Essentially it’s like inserting a straw into your nose,” Zeidan said. “You have a gag reflex, so most times people will gag, and that’s really uncomfortable. And people will even vomit repeatedly if it continues to irritate their gag reflex.”
Zeidan added that the forceful insertion of a feeding tube can lead to the swelling of the nostrils and the throat, and even tear them, leading to bleeding.

“It is like torture – somebody is doing a painful procedure to you that you don’t consent to,” Zeidan added. “Autonomy is a fundamental principle of medical ethics. We can’t do something to patients if they don’t want to, even if we think it’s good for them.”

There are numerous cells and rooms inside the Port Isabel medical unit, including isolation cells and shared rooms for ill detainees, according to Cora Perez. In recent weeks, there were five people in the Port Isabel medical isolation cells used for hunger striking or suicidal detainees, he added. He described the cells as “practically freezing”, constantly surveilled with a security camera, and with just a bed, toilet and sink. As well as himself, he says he observed the Uzbek man, a Middle Eastern man, a “tall” eastern European man and a Black man of unknown nationality in the isolation cells. Unit detainees are escorted by facility staff to showers and sometimes receive yard and television access, he said.

blocks.caption: A security guard at Port Isabel. Photograph: Verónica G Cárdenas/AFP via Getty Images

blocks.text: Cora Perez worries for the other detainees. The Black man, whose identity or nationality he does not know, seems to have “serious mental health problems”, Cora Perez observed.
“He harms himself and spends the night yelling and hitting the door, and does not let anyone sleep,” he said.

The Guardian has independently confirmed the eastern European and Middle Eastern men’s identities, but is not publicly naming them because efforts to contact them have been unsuccessful. DHS did not comment on the other men inside the medical isolation unit, saying they could not comment without the Guardian providing their identities.

Cora Perez had left his son and parents in Cuba and requested asylum at the Mexico-US border in 2023, according to a relative who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity due to fear of retaliation by immigration authorities. Cora Perez went to live with the relative in Florida, where he worked in maintenance at a hotel and as a food delivery worker, he said.

In March 2025, Cora Perez was arrested by local police and later convicted of two misdemeanors, including “breach of peace” and “obstructing an officer without violence”, according to local records. He was sentenced to two months in jail, his relative said. But ICE placed a hold on him and as he was being released in June 2025, immigration officials took him into custody – a common system – and soon transferred him to the Adelanto detention center, a privately-run facility in California.

Days in Adelanto turned to weeks, then months, then a over year, according to a federal court order denying one of his petitions requesting his release. His multiple requests to immigration and ordinary federal courts for release from detention, while he fights his asylum case, have been unsuccessful.

“All his claims will be heard by an immigration judge, and he will receive due process. This administration will not ignore the rule of law,” DHS said. “Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the US.”
In August, he stopped eating to protest against his protracted detention.

“I have spent two birthdays behind ICE’s bars,” he wrote. “The reasons I did the hunger strike in Adelanto are for my political asylum, for the time I have spent detained, [and] because I have a 14-year-old son who is starving to death in Cuba because he does not have my help.”
“Also due to the mistreatment by the officials,” he added.

Cora Perez did not tell his family about the hunger strike, so as not to further worry them. It was not until he was transferred to Port Isabel in late September that he confessed to his relative he had been on a prolonged hunger strike.
“He doesn’t share details so that I won’t get upset or worry,” the relative said in a phone interview.

blocks.caption: The barbed-wire fence at Port Isabel. Photograph: Verónica G Cárdenas/Reuters

blocks.text: Cora Perez’s mother, who is in Cuba, “does not know anything, because she is sick, and with his detention she has gotten worse”, the relative added, between tears. “I don’t want her nor his grandmother to know anything about it,” the relative added.

On October 30, the federal prosecutors requested permission for ICE to forcibly feed and hydrate Cora Perez. Hours later, a federal judge approved the procedures without hearing from Cora Perez. Cora Perez told the Guardian in various instances he felt it was unfair he was not given the opportunity to present his case to the judge before the judge approved his force-feeding.

“It’s very disturbing because the judge is basically making a decision on information that is only provided by one side,” said Linus Chan, a professor of clinical law and the director of the detainee rights clinic at the University of Minnesota law school. “That just seems ridiculous.”
Cora Perez was force-fed the following day, he said in his messages and in a phone call, adding that he did not physically resist because he “had seen a lot of mistreatment of others detained”.
“[ICE does] what they want with us, whatever they want, because a federal judge gave them permission,” he added. “I have suffered on the island [of Cuba] and now at the hands of ICE.”

After asking Cora Perez about DHS’s denials that he was force-fed, he repeated that he was. “Brother, ICE says and does whatever they want. They deny, punish, retaliate and do everything at their own will. They have even sent Cubans to Africa,” he said.

The number of people detained by ICE has soared under the Trump administration. And due to policy and legal changes, tens of thousands of people are forced to stay in detention for long periods while they fight their immigration cases.
Chan, from the University of Minnesota, says prolonged detention and delays in their cases lead to logical conclusion. “That’s exactly when people protest,” he said.
“And the only form of protest, for many of these people, is a hunger strike,” he said.
As Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown continues and people are detained as a first resort while their cases play out, Chan said: “Hunger strikes will become more common.”

articles.title: Emails reveal how Trump allies pushed pardons for election deniers
articles.summary:
Former Trump lawyer urged justice department officials to seek pardons for those falsely claiming he won the 2020 presidential election in their states

In the fall of 2025, Cleta Mitchell, a…

blocks.text: In the fall of 2025, Cleta Mitchell, a key lawyer in Donald Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 presidential election, contacted a justice department official with an urgent request.

Criminal cases against people who signed certificates falsely claiming that Trump won the presidential election in their state – known widely as fake electors – were pending in Georgia, Michigan, Arizona, Nevada and Wisconsin. She knew the official, pardon attorney Ed Martin, was working on a memo outlining why those involved in the fake elector scheme should receive a presidential pardon.

Mitchell, a key figure in the movement to sow doubt about US elections, wanted the justice department to move forward with the pardons immediately before any of the cases went to trial. “Time is of the essence,” she wrote.

“If trials (and in the Michigan case, an appeal of the dismissal) are allowed to occur, the additional financial and emotional costs to these loyal Trump supporters will be enormous,” she added in the message, which was obtained by the watchdog group American Oversight via a Freedom of Information Act request, and provided to the Guardian. “It is essential that the pardons move forward as quickly as possible before trials are scheduled and before these defendants are subjected to further expense and mental anguish. Please let me know what else I can do to help get this done.”
Martin’s response to Mitchell’s email was brief. “Thank you for this,” he wrote. “Very helpful.”
While the president eventually did issue a blanket pardon to the fake electors weeks later, the pardon was largely symbolic and did not affect the state-level charges they faced.

The email exchange offers insight into the machinations that took place behind the scenes as key players in the election denial movement shaped the administration’s efforts to relitigate the 2020 election won by Joe Biden and to absolve loyalists of wrongdoing.

blocks.caption: Ed Martin speaks at an event at the Capitol in Washington on 13 June 2023.  Photograph: Amanda Andrade-Rhoades/AP

blocks.text: “While the pardons were federal, not for the ongoing state cases, the documents shed light on the extent to which Mitchell and other Trump allies were using their access to get President Trump to act. Protecting our democratic system requires ensuring that no one, regardless of political influence or proximity to power, is placed above the law,” said Chioma Chukwu, executive director of American Oversight.
A person close to the pardon effort said Martin had been pressing and working on the issue for months. Mitchell did not respond to a request for comment.

In Georgia, at the time, the criminal case against Trump and fake electors were pending before the prosecuting attorneys council after Fulton county district attorney Fani Willis was disqualified. Mitchell suggested that a federal pardon could get the case dismissed.

Other states, including Georgia, a slate of Republican electors had met privately and signed a certificate claiming Trump was the winner of the presidential election. Republicans sought to have those certificates recognized during the counting of the vote on 6 January 2021 – an effort that was unsuccessful.

“If the pardons are issued promptly, before a new prosecutor is appointed, the Council can move for dismissal of the only remaining charges in the case, being the charges against President Trump,” she wrote to Martin. The prosecutor who eventually took over the case dismissed the charges, though it was for reasons unrelated to the pardons Trump issued.

Mitchell’s interest in the Georgia case was notable. She was on the telephone call when Trump put pressure on Georgia secretary of state Brad Raffensperger to find enough votes to overturn the election. A special purpose grand jury in Georgia recommended criminally charging Mitchell for her involvement in the effort to overturn the election in the state, though she ultimately was never charged.

Mitchell is a key figure in the election denial movement that has spread since the 2020 election. She has helped organize a network of local activists who have spread false and misleading information about elections. She is also linked to organizations that have provided funding for groups that have spread misleading information about elections.

In Martin, Mitchell had a powerful ally. Prior to joining the justice department, he participated in the effort to overturn the 2020 election, speaking at a rally in Washington on 5 January 2021. “What they’re stealing is not just an election. It’s our future, and it’s our republic,” he said during the speech. On January 6, he posted on X: “I’m at the Capitol right now. Abd [sic] I was at the POTUS speech earlier. Rowdy crowd but nothing out of hand. Ignore the #FakeNews.”

Martin represented some of those charged for January 6, and served on the board of an organization that provided financial assistance to their families. Before being appointed pardon attorney, he served as the interim US attorney for the District of Columbia, a position from which he fired and demoted prosecutors who worked on January 6 cases.

Writing about the Arizona case, Mitchell urged a pardon before a grand jury could file charges, saying it would “be optimum to stop the persecution of these defendants, which include two of Charlie Kirk’s top lieutenants at TPUSA [Turning Point USA]”. Kirk had been slain in Utah only weeks earlier.

Summarizing the Michigan and Wisconsin cases, Mitchell wrote that a presidential pardon could save defendants further financial burden. “Some of them have already spent their retirement funds, mortgaged their homes to pay legal fees, and suffered significant emotional hardship over the past four years. Allowing a trial to proceed is simply unacceptable.”

The US constitution gives the president broad power to pardon people convicted of federal crimes. But not state ones. Nonetheless, Mitchell has publicly advanced a novel legal argument that a federal pardon for the fake elector scheme could wipe out the state charges.

“The U.S. Constitution created the presidential electors and the federal Electoral Count Act controls the proceedings by which the electors conduct their federal responsibilities,” she wrote in an op-ed in the Federalist in November 2025. “We can reach only one conclusion: These are not true state charges, these are not state actors, and the entire scheme to concoct some odd collection of purported violations of state law are a nullity.” Mitchell also publicly advocated for the pardons on X.
The Oversight Project, a rightwing group, published a memo in November 2025 making similar arguments.

Trump eventually did issue a blanket pardon for the fake electors on 10 November 2025, though those pardons didn’t legally affect the state-level cases. In Wisconsin, the criminal case against three architects of the fake elector scheme is still pending. The cases against fake electors in Arizona, Michigan and Nevada have stalled for reasons unrelated to the pardons.
The day Trump issued the blanket pardons, Martin received an email congratulating him on the pardons.
“It was a long project,” Martin wrote. “But I am glad we stuck the landing.”

articles.title: ‘I agree with the president’: incoming senator Abdul El-Sayed seeks to help Trump end military aid to Israel
articles.summary:
Michigan senator-elect also secured a meeting with JD Vance, who called him a ‘terrible evil’ in lead-up to election

The incoming US senator Abdul El-Sayed of

blocks.text: The incoming US senator Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan said that he and Donald Trump were in agreement about ending foreign military aid to Israel – and he hopes to find more common ground with the US president when he takes office.

“I agree with the president – I can’t believe I’m saying that – that we need to end foreign military aid that is unconditional to Israel, as well as Egypt and Saudi Arabia and Pakistan,” the senator-elect said.

In a surprise election day announcement, Trump told Fox News that the US would end military aid to Israel at the end of this year under an agreement reached with that country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.

“I think we need to be applying very basic international law to what Israel is and has been doing,” El-Sayed added. “We should not continue to be running cover for them at the UN, at the ICC, at the ICJ.”

blocks.caption: Abdul El-Sayed at a campaign event in Muskegon, Michigan, on 11 October 2026. Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

blocks.text: He said he wanted to see Congress change its posture on the US’s relationship with Israel, starting by making sure the Democratic caucus is no longer funded by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), a pro-Israel lobby that spent heavily against El-Sayed in his election.

The comments come after El-Sayed said he has secured a meeting with JD Vance. The senator would not share the agenda of the meeting, but confirmed that the vice-president’s chief of staff reached out to him after his election victory.

El-Sayed has goaded the Trump administration into working with him. In recent days, he created a shiny gold “TrumpCare” card and said that Trump can call Medicare for All “TrumpCare” if it will help expand healthcare to more Americans.
Vance regularly attacked El-Sayed on the campaign trail, calling the incoming senator a “terrible evil” and “corrupted”.
After El-Sayed won his race, he called Vance “habibi”, a term of endearment in Arabic, and joked about how the vice-president will have to preside over his swearing-in ceremony in January.

blocks.caption: Abdul El-Sayed greets supporters who were not able to attend his campaign event after it reached maximum capacity in Traverse City on 10 October 2026. Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

blocks.text: During an interview earlier this week on Fox, Vance said that if El-Sayed wants to work with the Trump administration “to make people’s lives better”, then he would find “very much a willing partner”.
El-Sayed, who will become the first Muslim US senator in January, overcame tens of millions of dollars spent against him, first in a closely watched primary and then a swing-state general election.

He has three immediate goals once he’s sworn in, he told the Guardian: stopping the “nuclear bomb” of Medicaid cuts, ending the war in Iran and addressing the “stupid approach” to tariffs. He also plans to propose Medicare for All legislation, get to work on voting rights legislation after the US supreme court gutted the Voting Rights Act, advance the Pro Act to expand union rights and overturn Citizens United, the supreme court decision that unleashed unfettered outside spending on campaigns.

El-Sayed is supporting the Maryland senator Chris Van Hollen’s bid for the Senate leadership role. El-Sayed said Van Hollen, an advocate for Palestinian rights, would be an “amazing leader, and he’s a departure from a lot of the instincts of the past”. Van Hollen was an early supporter of El-Sayed in his primary election against the US representative Haley Stevens and campaigned for El-Sayed.

As part of his campaign promise to change the Washington establishment, El-Sayed said he would not be moving his family to the US capital, and would be spending a lot of time back in Michigan doing town halls and talking to voters.

blocks.caption: Abdul El-Sayed arrives at a press conference in Detroit on 22 September 2026. Photograph: Sarah Rice/Getty Images

blocks.text: El-Sayed has two young daughters. He’s one of a large group of incoming senators and representatives who skewed younger this cycle and also have young children. The “somewhat erratic” schedule of the job makes it harder on people with kids, he said, so making the US Capitol building a “free and open place” for children would help. The Capitol should help “good senators and congresspeople also be good parents”, he said.

“I think one of the challenges with service is that we forget that every public servant is a private servant too, and that’s to their families, in particular to their children,” El-Sayed said. “And those two things shouldn’t be mutually exclusive.”

Throughout his campaign, El-Sayed faced Islamophobic rhetoric, including from Trump and Republican officials. Though his campaign wasn’t about defending himself, Michiganders rejected those attacks when they voted him in, and that was important, he said.

“There are a lot of kids who are watching,” he said. “And when the president of the United States is attacking somebody for their name or how they pray, it’s important that the people of the state of Michigan stood up and said, ‘No, this is not how we want to be.’ And I think they sent a message that was loud and clear, and I’m really grateful for that.”

articles.title: Senate ethics panel to Bato dela Rosa: Respond to prolonged absence complaint
articles.summary: The Senate committee on ethics and privileges has transmitted to Senator Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa the complaint lodged against him due to his prolonged absence.

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 7:00pm
The Senate committee on ethics and privileges has transmitted to Senator Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa the complaint lodged against him due to his prolonged absence.

The Wag Kang KuCorrupt group on Friday posted the panel's transmittal letter to Dela Rosa on Facebook. Committee chair Senator Tito Sotto, who signed the document dated October 22, 2026, later confirmed the complaint to reporters.

"This is to inform you of the action taken by the Senate Committee on Ethics and Privileges… on the complaint filed by Wag Kang KuCorrupt, represented by Barry Gutierrez, Cielo Magno, et al., against you for alleged prolonged absence from official duties," the document read.
The ethics panel gave Dela Rosa 15 days upon receipt of the complaint to provide his written response and any information regarding the matter.
Dela Rosa started missing Senate engagements in 2025 following reports that the International Criminal Court (ICC) had issued an arrest warrant against him.

He resurfaced on May 11, but left Senate custody in the early morning of May 14 after a shooting incident erupted inside the legislative chamber's premises. He has not been seen publicly ever since, and now faces a P50-million bounty for information leading to his arrest.

According to the transmittal, Wag Kang KuCorrupt's initial complaint was filed as early as February 25, but it was returned after the panel found it did not comply with rules. Supplemental affidavits to support the complaint were later submitted on September 14.
The panel then deemed the complaint "in substantial compliance, both in form and in substance" during an executive session on October 22, the same date of the letter.

"You (Dela Rosa) are invited to provide the Committee with any information relevant to the complaint, including a written response, within 15 days from receipt of this notice. A copy of the complaint, the Supplemental Affidavits, and the Rules is attached for your reference," the document read.
The group's petition reasoned that Dela Rosa's prolonged absence showed a dereliction of duty and a grave abuse of privilege.

"Under ordinary working conditions in both the public and private sectors, employees who fail to report for work without authorized leave are ordinarily subjected to disciplinary measures, including salary deductions, suspension, or even outright termination. Breadwinners across the country work tirelessly, often under difficult conditions, precisely because their families' welfare depends on daily accountability and performance," the group's original complaint read. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: International court's ruling on Myanmar genocide means little for victims, but much for future cases
articles.summary: Legal experts say the International Court of Justice's first ever finding of genocide committed by a state may also help shape how that case and others like it are decided in the future. Victims,…

image.caption: Judge Yuji Iwasawa, centre, president of the United Nation's International Court of Justice, reads the court's landmark judgment that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation. The ruling took place Thursday at the International Court of Justice in

blocks.text: World·Analysis

Legal experts say the International Court of Justice's first ever finding of genocide committed by a state may also help shape how that case and others like it are decided in the future. Victims, human rights activists and legal observers had hoped that the case, filed against Myanmar in 2019, would open a new pathway for delivering justice on the international stage.
Court's finding that Myanmar committed genocide provides little change for Rohingya victims

In the days after the world's top court was asked to weigh in on accusations of genocide against Myanmar, legal experts, activists and victims alike hoped the case might, for the first time in decades, open a new pathway for delivering justice on the international stage.

That was back in 2019. The International Court of Justice's finding seven years later that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority was indeed celebrated as recognition of the decades-long suffering of the Rohingya people. But it came at a high price.
"For the first time the world has heard the Rohingya," said John Jonaid, a survivor of the genocide who is now an Ottawa-based Rohingya journalist and human rights advocate.
"But at the same time, it's too late, I would say, for us to get any justice for our suffering."
Rohingyas hail UN top court ruling that Myanmar guilty of genocide
The Myanmar military conducted "clearance operations" in Rakhine state in 2017, systematically destroying Rohingya villages, perpetrating brutal sexual violence and killing thousands of people.
Most Rohingya now live in the world's largest refugee camp in Bangladesh and beyond, with little prospect of return.

items: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya ethnic minority, International Court of Justice rules

blocks.text: In its judgment, the ICJ demanded that Myanmar provide reparations and allow Rohingya to return to their villages — but most of those villages have been erased, and the country's leadership has long disregarded international scrutiny, rejecting allegations of genocide.

The tension between a legal victory in the case against Myanmar, launched by the Muslim-majority African nation of Gambia, and the reality for Rohingya victims of genocide was inevitable from the start: while the court has the power to hear and rule on cases filed by states against other states, it has no real means with which to implement its rulings.

Gambia's Justice Minister and Attorney General Dawda Jallow, right, with lawyer Arsalan Suleman, speaks to the media after International Court of Justice ruling in The Hague, Netherlands, on Thursday. Gambia launched the proceedings at the court in 2019. (Patrick Post/The Associated Press)
And yet even before the Thursday ruling, the case still had a profound legal impact.

Five new cases involving genocide were subsequently filed at the ICJ, each with its own unique circumstances. They include the highly anticipated case brought forward by South Africa against Israel, accusing it of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza following Hamas's attacks on Oct. 7, 2023.

items: South Africa accuses Israel of 'genocidal' acts in Gaza; Israel rejects filing to top UN court 'with disgust'
As UN court prepares to hear genocide claim against Israel, Canada still hasn't taken a position

blocks.text: And now, legal experts say, the court's first ever finding of genocide committed by a state may also help shape how that case and others like it are decided in the future.
Not everyone agrees on exactly how.

At minimum, Thursday's ruling — the first of its kind at the ICJ — has brought the 1948 UN convention on genocide "back to life," said Canadian human rights lawyer Payam Akhavan, one of the attorneys who served as counsel for Gambia in the case.

"This is a landmark judgment of the ICJ, and it comes at a crucial point in the evolution of international law, including unprecedented attacks against both the international court and the ICJ," he said in an interview with CBC.

While Akhavan says the ruling is "grossly inadequate" in addressing the immediate plight of the victims of Myanmar's genocide, he notes that how the court has interpreted the law in this case could still play a role in shaping the outcome of future ones.

Canadian human rights lawyer Payam Akhavan, centre, sits at Gambia's counsel table for the January 2020 reading of the first International Court of Justice judgment on urgent measures concerning Myanmar. (Submitted by Payam Akhavan)
Ruling underlines sexual violence is a genocidal act

Significantly, the majority of the judges in the Myanmar case rejected the country's argument that the "clearance operations" it conducted against the Rohingya in 2017 were defensive military operations aimed at neutralizing a threat and therefore precluded genocide.
Priya Pillai, a lawyer and international law specialist, told CBC News the court ruled that "the fact that you have a conflict doesn't preclude the fact that you might have genocidal intent as well."
"The two things can exist at the same time."

Other strands of the ruling, says Akhavan, demonstrated an expansive approach to the genocide convention, which was adopted in the wake of the Holocaust and the murder of millions of Jews during the Second World War.

Crucially, the ICJ judges strongly affirmed that genocidal acts were not limited to murder or displacement, but could also include crimes of sexual violence and attacks on reproductive capability to prevent procreation.
Breaking down the ICJ's first-ever ruling on state genocide
Countless Rohingya women reported a campaign of mutilation and brutal sexual violence at the hands of Myanmar's military forces.

Marianne Vitug, legal advisor for the Global Justice Center, said at a news conference in The Hague Thursday that the court looked at how sexual violence was directed at women and girls of reproductive age and sometimes pregnant women, and how young and unmarried women were targeted with extreme and brutal violence.
"The targeting of reproductive capacity is now very clearly a genocidal act, so that is a significant finding in this case."

items: UN report condemns sexual violence by Myanmar military against Rohingya

blocks.text: Vitug says the court's reliance on evidence gathered by NGOs and fact-finding missions is also "very significant in relation to upcoming cases that will rely on similar findings."

Unlike in other cases, NGOs cannot intervene directly in cases before the ICJ. Only member states can do so, and in Gambia's case, that included Canada, jointly with France, the Netherlands, Denmark, Germany and the U.K., supporting Gambia's effort to end Myanmar's impunity.
Their intervention focused on how the court should interpret the genocide convention, including the role of sexual violence.
In 2018, Parliament voted unanimously to recognize that Myanmar's military actions against Rohingya people constituted genocide.
John Jonaid, a survivor of the genocide who is now an Ottawa-based Rohingya journalist and human rights advocate. (Nicole Williams/CBC)
A 'painfully long' process

Rohingya activists are skeptical that pressure by the international community will do anything to persuade Myanmar's current president, Min Aung Hlaing, who led the military during its operations in Rakhine State, to accept them back.
There is also the question of what they would be returning to.
"Their entire villages have been burned and their history has been erased from Myanmar, as if they never existed [there]," said Jonaid.
"There is no trace."

items: Rohingya man whose mother was abducted calls for refugee pathway to Canada

blocks.text: While they await the right conditions for return, Jonaid says countries like Canada that have taken an interest in the plight of Rohingya must do whatever possible to ensure they thrive — including providing opportunities for education and employment wherever they currently live.
Akhavan suspects meaningful change in the international justice system will take time.
"We have to understand that the fight for universal human rights is a painfully long historical process."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Nahlah Ayed is the host of the nightly CBC Radio program IDEAS. A veteran of foreign reportage, she's spent nearly a decade covering major world events from London, and another decade covering upheaval across the Middle East. Ayed was previously a parliamentary reporter for The Canadian Press. She has received several awards for her journalism, including the 2025 Edward. R. Murrow Award.

articles.title: Sara Duterte trial dates on Nov. 26 and 27 reset over defense witnesses' unavailability
articles.summary: Escudero initially listed November 26 and 27, as well as December 1 to 4, and then December 7 to 11 as trial dates. If needed, additional dates could be added before December 18. However, lead…

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 6:56pm

Day 45 of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial ended with a brief, tense moment as Senate impeachment presiding officer Francis Escudero announced the new schedule for the remainder of the year.

Escudero initially listed November 26 and 27, as well as December 1 to 4, and then December 7 to 11 as trial dates. If needed, additional dates could be added before December 18. However, lead defense counsel Sheila Sison raised a concern about the schedule.

“Our next witnesses are not available on 26 and 27, also given that we were only informed today that there will be hearings for next week, and as you know your honor, this is not our only commitment, so we have also already made some commitments in our other engagements,” Sison said.

“We are not interested in a protracted, prolonged trial of this case. And as this court has seen, the defense has been prudent with the time of this court has not abused this court, and has not wasted three months of time for presenting witnesses,” she added.
House prosecutor Terry Ridon moved to strike off the record Sison’s statement on wasting time, but the latter argued that it was a fact.
“It was not wasted, your honor. That needs to be clear,” Ridon said.
Escudero would later ask Sison to revise her statement from “waste” to “spend a lot of time.” Sison agreed.

“We cancel the 26 and the 27 given the fact that counsel for the respondent and witnesses are not available… We shall resume witness when your witness will be available on December 1. And we shall have four trial dates that week: 1, 2, 3 and 4.”
There will also be five trial days in the following week as needed, Escudero said. The trial is set from 10:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m.

“It is my hope that we can decide, one way or another, on this matter and on this case before we adjourn as a Congress and before the year is over. Again, one way or the other, so that both as a country and as a people, we can move forward accordingly, whatever the outcome of the trial may be,” Escudero said. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Nearly 600 women killed in South Africa within three months
articles.summary: Police officials called for "greater efforts to prevent... violence" against women and children.

blocks.text: Nearly 600 women were killed in South Africa between July and September this year, according to the country's latest crime statistics.
This figure includes 13 women whose partially naked and bruised bodies were found dumped in public areas in and around Johannesburg.
The murders triggered national outrage and police faced pressure to find the culprits, in a country with one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and murder rates in the world.
In the latest shocking killing, five women and a toddler were gunned down in Free State province earlier this week.
The latest crime statistics, released on Friday, revealed that 581 women were killed in the country between July and September, including 131 in the Gauteng province which includes Johannesburg.
The same statistics revealed a slight decline in the number of murders.
Police reported 5,590 murders, 204 fewer than in the same period last year. This still come to an average of about 60 murders a day.

It is not clear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease because the police had stopped giving these figures recently due to what they said were "significant anomalies" in the statistics.
Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said there needed to be "greater efforts to prevent... violence" against women and children.
According to police in Free State province, south of Johannesburg, three masked men opened fire on a family in the township of Botshabelo on Wednesday night.
The trio were allegedly looking for the owner of the house and when they realised he was not there, "forced their way into the house and started shooting at the people inside", police said.
The owner's wife was also shot in the stomach and was taken to hospital. No arrests have been made.
On Thursday, the police chief for Gauteng province said that eight people had now been arrested in relations to the 13 murders which sparked a national outcry earlier this year.
General Tommy Mthombeni said three of the arrests related to the murder of Elizabeth Moselakgomo, an avid runner whose disappearance prompted a highly publicised nationwide search for her.
The 38-year-old went missing while out for her daily run near her home in Kempton Park.
Her body was found badly bruised and partially clothed on 12 September.

The police chief said two other people had been detained in connection with the death of Jabulile Ntimba, 33, who was discovered half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Boksburg on 17 September. Ntimba's was the ninth body found in the Ekurhuleni region.
He said another person had been arrested for one of the Kempton Park cases while a suspect was arrested over Ntombifuthi Nxumalo's death in Tembisa, north-east of central Johannesburg.
Nxumalo was discovered at a cemetery on 26 September. She was found naked with serious head injuries as well as stones near her body.
Another arrest was made back in July, in relation to the death of Busisiwe Mahlangu, whose body was found in Kempton Park on 15 July. Hers was the first of the 13 bodies discovered in the area.
In September, President Cyril Ramaphosa vowed that "no stone will be left unturned" to find those behind the killings.
Last year, he declared that violence against women was a "national disaster".

articles.title: Cale88 had no employees in 2024, only 2 in 2025 — BOI records
articles.summary: Cale88 Foods Corp., a banana chips exporter co-founded by Vice President Sara Duterte’s husband, Manases Carpio, had no employees in 2024 and only two in 2025.

blocks.text: November 20, 2026 | 6:50pm
Department of Trade and Industry Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo testifies during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte at the Senate on Nov. 20, 2026.
Senate of the Philippines / Philstar.com's screenshot

MANILA, Philippines — Cale88 Foods Corp., a banana chips exporter co-founded by Vice President Sara Duterte’s husband, Manases Carpio, had no employees in 2024 and only two in 2025, company records presented during Duterte’s impeachment trial on Friday, November 20, showed.

Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo, who also serves as vice chairman and managing head of the Board of Investments (BOI), confirmed the figures during cross-examination by House prosecution counsel Erwin Matib.

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero allowed Matib to show Rodolfo Cale88's 2024 and 2025 General Information Sheets (GIS) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Rodolfo said he was familiar with the documents.
Asked how many rank-and-file employees the company had in 2024, Rodolfo answered, "Wala po" (None).
Matib followed up by asking if Cale88 had any manpower complement that year. Rodolfo said it had none.
The company's 2024 GIS listed three officers but no rank-and-file employees. Its 2025 filing listed two officers and two employees.
Rodolfo said the BOI had copies of the GIS because registered businesses are required to submit these documents to the agency.
The figures were raised as the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) had earlier reported that Cale88 recorded at least P1 billion in sales at one point.
The AMLC also found that the company received P776 million in foreign remittances from 2022 to 2025, including P319 million from China.

Most of the inflows were flagged by banks as covered and suspicious transactions due to missing supporting documents, the absence of underlying trade or economic obligations and inconsistencies with the company's financial profile.
BOI figures differ from company filings
Rodolfo also testified that BOI records showed Cale88 had 201 employees in 2024 and 50 in 2025, figures that were far higher than those declared in its GIS filings.
Documents presented during the proceedings also showed that Cale88 later transferred 95% of its shares to Pikimong Pikimong Philippines Corp.
Matib also asked Rodolfo about the company's employee records, including its Social Security System (SSS) contributions and PhilHealth benefits.

Rodolfo said he had not seen Cale88's submissions on these matters. He explained that the BOI does not automatically require registered businesses to submit employee lists unless they apply for incentives.
"Ang pangbangga kasi namin iyong incentives. 'Pag nag-avail po sila ng incentive, hihingin po namin 'yun (list of employees)," Rodolfo said.
(Our basis for requiring those documents is the incentives. If they apply for incentives, we would ask for the list of employees.)
"Dahil hindi naman siya nag-avail na incentive, wala pong pangbangga ho," he added.
(Since the company did not avail itself of any incentives, we had no basis to require those documents.)
Rodolfo also said he had no personal knowledge of Cale88's actual business operations or whether its declared building had been completed. The company had reported that its building was 90% complete.
Cale88 named after co-founders
Cale88 was co-founded in 2012 by Carpio, Duterte's husband, and dentist Lourdes Lebosada, who is also Carpio's business partner.

Rodolfo confirmed that the company's name came from the surnames of its founders. "CA" stands for Carpio, while "LE" refers to Lebosada. The number 88 represents infinity, based on information provided by the BOI's Davao extension office.
Cale88's business operations and financial transactions are being examined in connection with questions over Duterte's declared wealth under Article II of the articles of impeachment.

articles.title: Anthropic’s post-debut stumble delivers reality check for AI trade
articles.summary: Anthropic could offer an early read on investor appetite for the sector after a turbulent stretch, with a sustained decline likely to deepen concerns over lofty valuations and massive AI spending

blocks.text: Anthropic could offer an early read on investor appetite for the sector after a turbulent stretch, with a sustained decline likely to deepen concerns over lofty valuations and massive AI spending

items: Anthropic shares fell 6% in premarket trading after a strong debut, raising concerns about investor enthusiasm for the AI sector and high valuations.
The stock's valuation is approximately $1.7 trillion, with analysts warning that the current price may not be sustainable and that volatility is expected in the coming weeks.
The IPO has drawn comparisons to SpaceX, with investors advised to be cautious due to potential market fluctuations and competition from major companies like Apple and OpenAI.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Anthropic shares fell 6% in premarket trading on Friday, November 20, pulling back after a strong market debut that vaulted the AI lab into the ranks of the most valuable US companies but failed to revive investor enthusiasm for the sector.

Widely seen as a proxy for the AI trade, Anthropic could offer an early read on investor appetite for the sector after a turbulent stretch, with a sustained decline likely to deepen concerns over lofty valuations and massive AI spending.
The stock was at $91.24, below Thursday’s close, giving Anthropic a fully diluted valuation of about $1.7 trillion and a market capitalization of $1.2 trillion based on shares outstanding.

The shares are likely to remain in focus for signs of volatility as the initial euphoria surrounding the listing fades and investors assess whether a valuation of about 40 times sales over the past 12 months can be sustained.

“A decline in share value is normal following a high-profile listing, but we don’t know if that decline will be in line with other IPOs or more volatile, and that should raise alarms for investors,” said Tejal Patel, executive director at the SOC Investment Group.
Anthropic shares closed on Thursday at 13% below their opening price, reinforcing concerns trading could remain volatile in the first few weeks as some investors seek quick gains.
“We would not describe the valuation as cheap. At this valuation, the growth plan is largely priced in,” said Harrison Rolfes, senior research analyst of private company coverage at PitchBook.
“Large IPOs have historically delivered modest returns in their first year.”
The focus now shifts to a potential OpenAI listing, which could provide the next major test of investor appetite for AI stocks. OpenAI has indicated it may go public next year.
Wall Street’s main indexes ended sharply lower on Thursday, and futures pointed to another day of declines on Friday.
Anthropic’s IPO has drawn parallels with Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which went public in June after the second-biggest IPO on record.

While the companies have different business models, some investors have pointed to SpaceX’s sharp swings in the weeks after its debut as a reason for caution over buying Anthropic immediately after its listing.

“There’s going to be some volatility like we had with SpaceX. A lot of people are going to have FOMO. I don’t think there’s any need to get on it on the first trade,” said Rob Hackel, CEO of financial advisory and brokerage firm RF Lafferty & Co.
Retail investors traded about $772 million of Anthropic shares on Thursday, the most for an IPO debut since Vanda Research began tracking the data in 2012.
Competition could also weigh on investor sentiment.

Apple is developing an AI agent that can perform tasks on behalf of users, entering a market already being pursued by OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta Platforms, Bloomberg News reported on Friday. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Tubig Pilipinas secures up to P900-million investment from Maharlika
articles.summary: The transaction is expected to give MIC a 9.9% ownership stake in Tubig Pilipinas if it invests the full P900 million

blocks.text: The transaction is expected to give MIC a 9.9% ownership stake in Tubig Pilipinas if it invests the full P900 million
MANILA, Philippines – Sovereign wealth fund Maharlika Investment Corporation (MIC) is investing up to P900 million in water utilities firm Tubig Pilipinas Holdings Inc.

MIC signed a convertible note agreement with Tubig Pilipinas on Friday, November 20, with an initial investment of P450 million. It comes with an option to put in another P450 million through a follow-on offering targeted for the first quarter of 2027.
The transaction is expected to give MIC a 9.9% ownership stake in Tubig Pilipinas if it invests the full P900 million.
According to its Philippine Stock Exchange disclosure, the funding will be used to “accelerate water infrastructure expansion,” particularly in underserved communities.

In a separate statement, MIC confirmed the agreement, with its outgoing president and chief executive Rafael “Joel” Consing Jr. describing the investment as part of the sovereign wealth fund’s strategy related to infrastructure.

“This partnership fits a deliberate pattern. Power for the islands. New port cities. Now, water. Power and water are what every community needs to function; ports are what connect them to growth,” Consing said.

blocks.caption: The Maharlika fund that Joel Consing leaves behind

blocks.text: Tubig Pilipinas operates water supply and distribution projects outside major metropolitan areas through its operating subsidiary, Tubig Pilipinas Group. Its portfolio includes water supply projects in Bacolod City, Negros Occidental, and water distribution systems in Trece Martires, Cavite; San Jose City, Nueva Ecija; Coron, Palawan; and Catbalogan, Samar.

The company itself is relatively new to the stock market in its present form, having completed a backdoor listing by acquiring the dormant Coal Asia Holdings earlier this year and rebranded it into TUBIG.
Its shares, however, have been suspended from trading since October 19 after a share-swap transaction reduced its public float to 10.64%, below the PSE’s 20% minimum requirement.
The Maharlika deal also comes just days before Consing’s term ends on November 23.
Consing earlier told reporters that MIC was working on two or three additional investments that could be announced before the end of 2026.

Since its establishment in 2023, Maharlika has invested in port operator Asian Terminals Inc., electricity-grid holding firm Synergy Grid and Development Philippines, and short-term financing for Petron, among others.

Still, the sovereign wealth fund has been exceedingly cautious in deploying its capital. As of end-September 2026, it had invested P24.7 billion, about a third of its initial P75 billion, while retaining P53.67 billion in cash and cash equivalents. – Rappler.com

articles.title: DepEd gives Antipolo teachers laptops, tech training
articles.summary: The Department of Education (DepEd) has launched a hands-on technology training program for public school teachers alongside its nationwide distribution of laptops, as part of efforts to accelerate…

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 6:18pm

The Department of Education (DepEd) has launched a hands-on technology training program for public school teachers alongside its nationwide distribution of laptops, as part of efforts to accelerate digitalization in basic education.

Education Secretary Sonny Angara led the launch of GuroXL, a customized professional development program, during the distribution of laptops to 1,441 public school teachers from 62 schools in Antipolo City.
The teachers received MacBook Neo laptops under the DepEd Computerization Program (DCP) and immediately participated in guided training sessions on how to use the devices for classroom instruction.

"What this is all about is giving you the best that we can give you. Because we know teachers give their best, even without laptops, you give everything you can and go above and beyond what is required. That is why you continue to inspire us, and the President is behind you one hundred percent. We at DepEd are behind you one hundred percent," Angara said.

“Please maximize these tools because there is so much that they can do for you and for your learners. Let us take time to listen because they will explain to you the potential, and they will make you more productive, save you time, and enable you to be a better teacher,” he added.
The rollout builds on the nationwide laptop distribution program launched by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Angara in Dagupan City on November 9.

DepEd has awarded contracts for 231,725 teacher laptops, consisting of 169,008 MacBook Neo units and 62,717 Windows-based laptops. Another 3,646 MacBook Neo units were procured for administrative officers.
The delivery and deployment of the devices are expected to continue through March 2027.

Coordinated through the National Educators Academy of the Philippines (NEAP), the DepEd Information and Communications Technology Service, and the Bureau of Learning Delivery, GuroXL allows teachers to train using the same laptops assigned to them.
The laptop packages were procured through competitive public bidding at approximately P43,000 per unit, significantly below suggested retail prices.
Each package includes a five-year warranty, built-in productivity software, logistics, technical support and professional development assistance.
DepEd said the nationwide rollout aims to narrow the digital divide in public education while reducing teachers' administrative workload.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: South Korea catches 111 students with new measures against exam cheating
articles.summary: The students were caught with banned smart devices while taking the high-stakes Suneung exam.

blocks.text: South Korea's education ministry says 111 candidates were found with unauthorised smart devices during a high-stakes nationwide exam, after officials introduced urgent measures to tackle rising cases of AI-assisted cheating.
Five of the candidates were caught red-handed using smart devices during the exam, authorities said on Friday.
Half a million students sat for the college entry exam, also known as Suneung, which took place this week under the shadow of several recent high-profile cheating scandals.
Prior to the Suneung, authorities announced anti-cheating measures such as emergency alerts sent to every single mobile phone in the country to detect unauthorised devices in exam halls.
On Friday, Prime Minister Lee Jae Myung called for an overhaul of the exam system to tackle AI-assisted cheating.

In South Korea, public examinations "significantly affect the distribution of opportunities and resources", Lee said, adding that using AI to cheat in such tests "rocks the basic order of our society by undermining fairness and trust".
Concerns over academic dishonesty had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.
Last month, two candidates were caught cheating with AI glasses during university entrance exams.
The education ministry said earlier this month that four students across middle and high schools were caught using AI glasses to cheat this year.
These fears came to a boil over the weekend, when the top scorer of South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam admitted to cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.
His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.

"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," said the candidate, 34-year-old Han Won-seok, in a video published on Sunday.
His confession, days ahead of the Suneung, prompted authorities to introduce last-minute measures to prevent cheating during the national exam.
The measures included nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.

Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.
The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.
It was the first time that South Korea tapped on its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.
Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.
All this made even honest test takers paranoid.
Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times that he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.
Another told news outlet Yonhap that he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.
Held every November, the Suneung is an infamous eight-hour marathon of back-to-back exams.
Students attempt about 200 questions across various subjects, which include Korean, maths, English, social and natural sciences, among others.
The country itself comes to a standstill - construction work halts, planes are grounded and military training gets suspended to facilitate an optimal testing environment.
Many South Koreans see the Suneung as a culmination of years of formal education - and a turning point that determines their university placements, careers, and social statuses.

articles.title: Can German auto manufacturing recover after Mercedes and VW cuts?
articles.summary: German automakers are pulling back on investments at home, sparking fresh anxiety about the auto sector's future. Some industry watchers think there is still a narrow window to stem the decline. But…

image.caption: Mercedes-Benz has halted all further investments in German manufacturing for the time being and is also weighing plant closuresImage: Bernd Weißbrod/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Mercedes-Benz's announcement last week that it would halt further investments at its factories in Germany has added to the sense that the country's best automaking days are behind it.
In a written interview for staff, production chief Michael Schiebe noted how the running costs of German plants are far too high.
Schiebe added that the automaker is "now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure."
The decision came one day after Volkswagen (VW), Europe's largest carmaker, said it was shelving plans to modernize its massive Wolfsburg plant.
Can crisis reinvent the car again?
German auto industry faces restructuring

Germany's auto sector is in a deep crisis, amid fierce rivalry from ambitious Chinese automakers. VW alone is looking to cut 100,000 jobs globally by 2030, while four of its German factories are earmarked for possible closure.
Yet, many auto analysts doubt this really marks the beginning of the end for car making in the country.

"We have to admit that a third of our capacity [in German plants] is overcapacity and that needs to be cut," Thomas Puls, senior economist for transport and infrastructure at the Cologne Institute for Economic Research (IW Köln), told DW. "This will hurt a lot."

A report last month by Munich-based consultancy Roland Bergeragreed that domestic automaking needs an urgent "reset," but predicted that Germany could still "preserve a sustainably profitable core of automotive value creation."
In other words, car making in Germany may shrink, but what remains could be leaner, more specialized and more profitable.

blocks.caption: In Germany, Mercedes has three assembly plants and seven facilities that manufacture drivetrains and componentsImage: Axel Schmidt/REUTERS

blocks.text: Unions dig in amid fight for survival

Many doomsayers overlook the fact that Mercedes' investment halt is tied to tough negotiations with unions over cutting labor costs at its German plants. This includes scrapping the 35-hour workweek. The investment freeze could be lifted if a deal is reached.
Even so, Achim Kampker, an electric mobility engineering professor at RWTH Aachen University, sees the investment cuts as more than a negotiating tactic.
Kampker compared China's lightning-fast industrial strategy with Germany's, which he said was "too slow," as excessive bureaucracy and complex business structures prevent value creation.
"We need to become faster, more innovative and significantly more productive," Kampker told DW.
China's EV-makers can bring a new model to market in around 20 months, versus 48 to 60 months for Germany, according to Roland Berger. Plus, the Chinese have a 30% cost advantage.
Production costs at German plants are also much higher — between €3,500 ($3,840) and €5,000 per vehicle — than in Eastern Europe, where they range from €2,000 to €2,500.

blocks.caption: Mercedes plans more than 40 model launches by next year — a growing share will be built outside GermanyImage: Joan Cros/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Does Germany have a 'false sense of security?'

A separate report by consultancy PwC in September noted that despite German carmakers being well managed, well capitalized and knowing exactly what is coming, they may have a "false sense of security."
PwC said Germany needs to focus on four areas to ensure its auto industry is "future-fit" to compete with China.

These include splitting its internal combustion engine (ICE) business from the electric vehicle (EV) business, investing bumper ICE profits into those new technologies, redesigning workplace culture and training, and leveraging existing partnerships with Chinese automakers and US tech firms.
"The future viability of the German automotive industry depends significantly on decisions made in the next 12 to 18 months," wrote Harald Wimmer, global and German automotive leader at PwC Germany.
With the transition to EVs, some predict that automaking will become part of a much larger global electronics sector, which Germany must exploit.

Wimmer noted how top Chinese automakers were already benchmarking themselves against consumer electronics giants. These include smartphone maker Xiaomi, which now also produces around 400,000 EVs per year.
"Anyone who continues to base their competitive framework solely on their own industry is making a mistake that cannot be corrected once it becomes apparent," he warned.
Production remains resilient despite decline
Despite all the doom and gloom, car production within Germany is holding up pretty well.

Domestic manufacturing sits around 12% lower than pre-pandemic levels. This year, however, the auto sector is on course to meet a December estimate of 4.11 million vehicles, just 1% lower than last year, according to the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA).
IW Köln's Puls thinks German automakers must now avoid a trap Italy fell into in the early 2000s when its national auto champion, Fiat, struggled with profitability.

In Italy, "the politics and the unions blocked any attempt by Fiat to cut overcapacity," Puls told DW. "What's the result? They have a capacity of 1.1 to 1.2 million cars and utilization of about 250,000."
Last year, those same Italian plants built just 214,000 passenger cars, according to the FIM Cisl trade union, the fewest since 1954.
Analysts call for faster reform
For Germany, the issue isn't a lack of expertise or ambition; it's that reforms to huge industries often get weighed down by caution and red tape.

As the country's auto giants try to push through painful cuts, RWTH Aachen University's Kampker warned that if they fail to address their shortcomings, "we will see more production sites closing and a substantial shift of industrial investment and employment away from Germany."
"There is still an opportunity to reverse this trend, but the window of opportunity is narrowing," Kampker concluded.
