articles.title: Global stock markets slump as Anthropic IPO fails to stem AI sell-off
articles.summary: Asian markets on track for their worst week since 2020, with European and US stocks also way down

blocks.text: Global stock markets have slumped as Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies.

Asian stock markets were on track for their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell on Friday. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chipmaker TSMC down about 6%.

In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.
European stock markets were heading for their worst week since March, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.3% in the first 90 minutes.
The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by over 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.

Anthropic’s shares jumped 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the frontier AI firm began. But they were heading for losses on Friday, down 6% at $91.30, falling back towards the IPO price of $83.

Anthropic’s floation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.

“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”
after newsletter promotion
Britain’s FTSE 100 share index hit a five-month low on Friday morning. It has dropped by 4.8% this week, and is heading for its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.

articles.title: Quezon residents seek answers over environmental risks of 50,000-hog piggery
articles.summary: Residents near a 50,000-hog piggery in San Antonio, Quezon, raise concerns over potential water contamination, threats to farms and livelihoods, and the lack of answers from government agencies

blocks.text: Conclusion

QUEZON PROVINCE, Philippines – For residents living near a sprawling piggery designed to accommodate up to 50,000 hogs, the concern is no longer just the loss of agricultural land. It is whether the facility’s waste management system can protect their water sources, farms, and livelihoods, and whether government agencies will act if those safeguards fail.

The 12-hectare development of Mighty Livestock Farms in Barangay Callejon, San Antonio, Quezon, has raised concerns among residents of surrounding communities who rely on nearby irrigation waterways and groundwater for farming and household use.
The project has also become a source of frustration for former rice farmhands who found temporary employment during its construction, only to abruptly lose their jobs.

blocks.caption: Ricefields to piggery: Questions over land conversion for 50,000-hog facility in Quezon

blocks.text: For Emma Alday, a resident in her eighties whose farm lies just 250 meters from the development, the controversy has become a prolonged struggle to obtain answers from government agencies responsible for protecting agricultural land, farmers, and the environment.
Beyond the loss of productive agricultural land, residents fear the environmental consequences of a facility designed to accommodate as many as 50,000 pigs.

Alday estimates that each hog could produce approximately five kilograms of waste daily. Using that figure, the facility could potentially generate as much as 250,000 kilograms, or 250 metric tons, of waste every day if operating at full stocking capacity.
“Siguradong maaapektuhan ang aming water. Kahit sabihin nilang modern na. The air, and the langaw. We will only find out when it starts,” Alday said.
(Our water will definitely be affected, even if they say the facility is modern. The air quality will also be affected, as well as attract flies.)
For residents who rely on nearby waterways for irrigation and groundwater for household use, these are not abstract concerns.
Former construction worker Arnel Las, who previously worked as a farmhand in the ricefields, said the proposed waste-treatment facilities are situated near agricultural areas and waterways.
“Yung tubigan namin mismong kalapit ng piggery. Yung lagoon ang nagpapatubig sa palay. Yung lagoon nila 20 meters, hindi nilagyan ng flooring, talagang lupa, kaya derecho yun sa palayan,” he alleged.

(Our irrigation waterway is right next to the piggery. The lagoon supplies water to the rice fields. Their lagoon is 20 meters and has no concrete flooring – it is just bare earth, so the water goes straight into the ricefields.)
Las also expressed concern about the potential impact on drinking water.
“Ang tubig na aming iniinom ay mula sa poso, kaya makakaapekto rin sa amin (The water we drink comes from a hand pump, so we will also be affected).”
According to Las, the communities potentially affected include barangays San Juan, San Francisco, Behia, Callejon, Sinturisan, and Briones, which he said share interconnected irrigation waterways.

Whether wastewater from the facility could seep into surrounding soil and groundwater, and whether its waste-treatment system can safely handle the expected volume, are among the questions residents want the Department of Environment and Natural Resources-Environmental Management Bureau (DENR-EMB) to answer.
The EMB issued an Environmental Compliance Certificate (ECC) for the project on October 24, 2023, covering a total land area of 113,973 square meters, or approximately 12 hectares.
The ECC identifies the development as a Livestock Farm Project with a maximum stocking capacity of 50,000 hogs at any given time.

However, an ECC does not, by itself, establish that a facility will have no adverse environmental impact. Rather, it sets environmental conditions and commitments with which the project proponent must comply.
For residents, the pressing question is whether those safeguards are sufficient and who will be held accountable if they fail.
The municipal government of San Antonio maintains that Mighty Livestock Farms has complied with the documentary requirements for its development.
In an interview, Sangguniang Bayan Secretary Carlo Katigbak said the municipality has mechanisms to act against establishments that violate environmental regulations.
“Although nabibigyan sila ng authority to operate, once na nagkaroon ng non-compliances, nagkakaroon ng immediate action talaga ang local government unit,” he said.
(Although they are granted the authority to operate, the local government unit takes immediate action once there are any instances of non-compliance.)
He added that the municipality could revoke a company’s license to operate or business permit if violations were established.

“In case magkaroon ng mga violation may mga recourse din ang municipio such as revocation of license to operate or business permit, mahigpit po ang local government sa mga ganitong bagay lalo na kung may kinalaman sa environment.”

(In case of violations, the municipality has recourse, including revoking the license to operate or the business permit. The local government is strict on these matters, especially when they involve the environment.)
The assurances, however, have not dispelled residents’ concerns about the potential impact on irrigation waterways, groundwater, and neighboring farms.
The controversy has also taken a human toll on former rice farmers who found temporary employment during the first two years of the piggery’s construction.
Las said he and other residents initially believed that a feed mill would be built on the property.
“Ang sabi nila ay feedmill ang itatayo, nung binubuo na, piggery na (They said a feed mill would be built, but by the time construction began, it was a piggery),” he said.
After working on the construction site for nearly two years, Las said he and several other workers were abruptly dismissed.
“Kami po ay tinanggal ng walang sinabi. Nakatira doon mismo sa sitio na pinagtrabahuhan namin. Kami rin ang mga dating farmhands sa ricefields.”
(We were dismissed without being given any explanation. We lived right there in the sitio where we worked. We were also former farmhands in the ricefields.)
He said some employment benefits, including their 13th-month pay, remained unsettled at the time of the interview.

“Nag-report po kami sa San Antonio Mayor’s Office noong September, sabi sa amin tatawagan kami pero hanggang ngayon ay wala naman tumawag sa amin. Lumapit din kami sa aming barangay kagawad pero wala din.”

(We reported the matter to the San Antonio Mayor’s Office in September. We were told they would call us, but no one has contacted us to this day. We also approached our barangay councilor, but nothing came of it.)
Another former worker, Kenneth Ocampo, said 16 workers were dismissed after being told that the company needed to reduce its workforce because of financial constraints.

“Nagbabawas daw po sila ng trabahador dahil wala na silang pasahod. Ngayon nabalitaan namin, nagdadagdag naman sila. Sabi kasi priority kaming mismong taga doon, pero bakit naman po kami pa mismo ang tinanggal. Ang tinira nila ay yung mga taga malayong lugar,” he lamented.

(They said they were reducing their workforce because they could no longer afford to pay the workers. Now we’ve heard they are hiring more people. They said residents from the area would be given priority, so why were we the ones who were dismissed? They kept workers from faraway places.)
He said the workers were never given a clear explanation for their dismissal.
“Siguro po may nagawa kaming mali, pero hindi naman dapat na basta-basta na lang kami tatanggalin, dapat kausapin nila kami kung bakit.”
(Maybe we did something wrong, but they shouldn’t have just dismissed us without explanation. They should have talked to us and told us why.)
Today, Ocampo survives on occasional jobs, a far cry from the regular income he once earned.
The workers’ accounts raise additional questions about the impact of the development on residents who previously depended on the land for their livelihoods.
As early as three years ago, Alday and other concerned residents began organizing opposition to the project.
They gathered approximately 300 signatures from residents of San Antonio and neighboring Tiaong and sent a petition to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr..
“Ang pangunahing pagkain natin ay BIGAS (Our staple food is rice),” the petition emphasized, warning of the continuing loss of ricefields.
The appeal, dated November 28, 2024, did reach the national government.

A memorandum dated January 27, 2025, signed by DAR-Calabarzon Director Cupido Gerry Asuncion, documents the referral of Alday’s complaint from the Presidential Action Center through the DAR Central Office to the provincial office in Quezon.
The memorandum specifically directed the provincial office to respond to Alday and report any action taken. But Alday says the referral has not resulted in a satisfactory response.
“So I was asking the DAR people kung ano ang gagawin nilang pagkilos, eh ang dami daw nilang ginagawa kaya hindi nila mabigyan ng attention up to now, so wala,” she recalled.
(So I asked the DAR personnel what action they would take, but they said they had so much work that they had been unable to attend to the matter up to now. So nothing has happened.)
She also approached the EMB office in Lucena, whose personnel visited the project site and inspected the biogas and lagoon facilities.
“Yung EMB na Lucena all they do is investigate and report to the region (The EMB office in Lucena only investigates and reports to the regional office),” she said.
For Alday, the visits, referrals, and repeated follow-ups have yet to produce clear answers to the concerns she has raised.
The difficulty in obtaining answers is not confined to the affected residents.

In an effort to establish the facts and present all sides, Rappler contacted the Department of Environment and Natural Resources–Environmental Management Bureau (DENR-EMB) IVA, the National Irrigation Administration (NIA) in Quezon, the Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR) Quezon, and Mighty Livestock Farms through email and/or phone.

Rappler subsequently followed up with all four parties on several occasions. Yet more than two weeks after the initial inquiries, none had responded to questions concerning matters that fall directly within the mandates of the government offices approached or to the allegations involving the company’s development.

For Alday, the fight has become an exhausting search for accountability. She has spent the past two years writing letters, visiting government offices, following up on referrals, and asking questions she believes should have been answered long ago. Her efforts have taken her from local offices to regional agencies and even to the Office of the President.

Yet the central questions remain unanswered. How was irrigated riceland allowed to give way to a 50,000-head piggery? Were the farmers’ rights adequately protected? Were surrounding communities properly informed and consulted? Can the facility’s waste-management system safeguard the waterways and groundwater on which nearby residents depend?

And perhaps most importantly, why has it been so difficult for ordinary citizens to obtain clear explanations from the very institutions mandated to protect agricultural land, farmers, and the environment?
For Alday and the residents who joined her appeal, the answers remain elusive even as the development that prompted their concerns continues to take shape. – Rappler.com

articles.title: They finally had their dream food truck. Then it was repossessed
articles.summary: A family ran their business, LeoMay Fusion, out of a food truck for about a year in rural Nova Scotia until RCMP officers showed up in mid-October and they learned a previous lender was repossessing…

image.caption: Leonardo Illas Jr., his wife Dayarit Duarte, his mother Maylin Rodriguez and his father Leo Illas now work out of the arena in Oxford, N.S. (Elizabeth McMillan/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia·New

A family ran their business, LeoMay Fusion, out of a food truck for about a year in rural Nova Scotia until RCMP officers showed up in mid-October and they learned a previous lender was repossessing the vehicle.
Family business, LeoMay Fusion, found second-hand truck on Facebook Marketplace
While Maylin Rodriguez prepares lunch service in Oxford, N.S., she worries about how her family will repay a loan for a food truck it no longer has.

Rodriguez and her family had run their business, LeoMay Fusion, out of the food truck for about a year in rural Nova Scotia before RCMP officers showed up in mid-October and they learned a previous lender was repossessing the second-hand vehicle.

"We were like, this can't be happening. We paid for this truck. We think that we did things properly. They just let us know that the person who sold it to us had no right to sell the truck,” she said.
“We were devastated. Still in this disbelief.”

Rodriguez and her husband, son and daughter-in-law now serve customers out of the canteen in the community’s arena. They are open seven days a week, trying to repay the approximately $65,000 they borrowed to buy the truck, outfit it and get the business up and running.
The family travelled to Quebec to buy the truck and then operated for about a year after upgrading it. (LeoMay Food Truck/Facebook)
But they say their sales at the canteen are less than 10 per cent of what they earned serving dishes inspired by their Cuban and Venezuelan roots at events around the region.

They bought the food truck in Quebec after connecting with a seller on Facebook Marketplace. From the start, they said, it didn’t operate as promised and they had to upgrade the water system and deep fryer.

The family, who came to Canada in the past decade, said they had a steep learning curve — from figuring out how to do the accounting and taxes to sourcing the food and cooking quality meals quickly. They did plenty of research and asked other businesses for advice, said Leonardo Illas Jr., Rodriguez’s son.
"At first it was just a dream, then working toward getting things going, then suddenly you're there and it's fantastic but it's definitely challenging,” he said.
The family that operates LeoMay Fusion took their food truck to events across Nova Scotia and to other parts of the Maritimes. (Submitted by LeoMay Fusion)
It was a dream that ended abruptly when they learned there was a lien against the truck in Quebec. It wasn’t caught when they registered the vehicle in Nova Scotia.
Now the family wants to warn others to take precautions when buying second-hand goods.
Up to purchaser to search for liens

Lenders and some companies, like garages, can place liens on a vehicle, allowing them to repossess it if debts go unpaid. Liens can also be applied to mobile homes, boats, off-road vehicles and tractors.

The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre said in a statement it’s important for buyers to do due diligence, including verifying a seller’s information, confirming ownership and checking for outstanding liens or financial claims.

Rodriguez said they took their bill of sale to the Société de l'assurance automobile du Québec, which handles vehicle registration in Quebec, and were told they could proceed with registering it in Nova Scotia. She said no one mentioned checking for liens there or when they registered it.
The Nova Scotia Registry of Motor Vehicles requires a certificate signed from a past owner, but it is not responsible for checking for liens, a spokesperson told CBC News.
There is a site that for a fee searches for liens across the territories and Atlantic Canada using a vehicle’s identification number (VIN). Quebec and other provinces have separate systems.
Leonardo Illas Jr., left, says his father Leo Illas Sr., right, has been applying to jobs. (Elizabeth McMillan/CBC)

Dealerships are responsible for checking for liens before they sell used vehicles, but the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada warns that the rules around whether private sellers must disclose liens vary by province. It advises people to check for liens themselves through online personal property searches.
Rodriguez said her family didn’t know the right questions to ask and learned too late about the importance of checking for liens.
“What about new Canadians, newcomers, young people that don't know and they want to … [be] entrepreneurs? It would be great if they can have some guidance,” said Rodriguez.
“We come here, we learn English, we learn new rules, but we can't learn [it] all. And I think the institutions should offer as much information as they can so we can be prepared."
Considering legal action
Rodriguez said they’ve shared all the documentation they have with police in Longueuil, Que. The force said it is reviewing the incident and there have been no criminal charges.

RCMP in Nova Scotia declined to comment as they are not the lead agency. Their only involvement was being there as a safety precaution when the truck was repossessed, and a spokesperson said lenders often ask for their presence.
Meanwhile, the family is still on the hook for the money they borrowed. They said they’ve consulted a lawyer in Quebec but don’t know if they can afford to take any legal action.

The Cumberland branch of the Community Business Development Corporation, which issued their loan, said in a statement that they “recognize the difficult circumstances facing the business owners,” but declined to comment on the case.

Maylin Rodriguez, who is originally from Cuba, hopes lenders and other organizations consider that newcomers don't always know the right questions to ask when starting businesses. (Elizabeth McMillan/CBC)
The LeoMay Fusion team had hoped to operate the canteen and food truck concurrently this winter. Instead, they had to cancel commitments to community groups, who they thanked for being understanding.
“We served large events. We had the whole season scheduled, so we were counting on that revenue. But then [we] changed to here,” Rodriguez said at the canteen.
“We've seen a significant drop in our earnings, which is understandable because it's a small town.”
'Heartbreaking to hear what happened'

Ongoing repairs at the Oxford rink mean there is currently no ice surface, resulting in slower days at the canteen. The family said they’ve been grateful for the support of loyal customers like Emme Bidwell, who stopped in on Monday, picking up a chicken and pork rice bowl.
“It’s one of my favourite meals,” Bidwell said. "It's just heartbreaking to hear what happened. But anything we can do to support our local small restaurants."
LeoMay Fusion has a takeout window in the arena in Oxford, N.S. (Elizabeth McMillan/CBC)
Illas already works a second job. His father is looking for one.
“It's been a lot — having to apply for jobs, having to deal with lawyers, having to deal with the police … cancelling events,” said Illas.
Rodriguez said she understands they may never get their money back, and hopes lenders and other organizations consider their story and ways to better support other newcomers.

blocks.text: “Of course we want justice for our family. We would like to recover what we lost," she said.

"But if we can prevent someone else, another family, newcomer, new Canadian, someone trying to build a business, to go through the same pain that we're going [through], then speaking publicly is worth it,” added Rodriguez.

articles.title: Russian attacks on Kyiv kill 3, cripple bridges and cut power
articles.summary: Russia launched missiles and drones across Kyiv overnight that killed three people, injured nine others and damaged bridges and transport infrastructure, local authorities said Friday.

image.caption: A man walks through debris at the site of a warehouse that was struck during a Russian drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv, Ukraine, November 20, 2026. (Thomas Peter/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New
Russia launched missiles and drones across Kyiv overnight that killed three people, injured nine others and damaged bridges and transport infrastructure, local authorities said Friday.
Missile, drone strikes came after Putin vowed to retaliate for attacks on key bridge to Crimea

The attacks came hours after President Vladimir Putin vowed to retaliate against Ukraine for three aerial attacks this week on the vital Kerch Bridge, which links occupied Crimea with the Russian mainland.

items: With Putin in the room, Carney condemns Russia's illegal invasion of Ukraine

blocks.text: "We will respond to these attacks, and I want everyone to be clear about that," Putin told reporters Thursday in China, where he attended a summit with the Chinese and U.S. presidents. Putin said the road side of the bridge had been "seriously damaged" and vowed to rebuild.

The Kyiv City Military Administration said the attack struck four districts of the capital. The attack caused widespread electricity disruptions. Energy provider DTEK said parts of the Pecherskyi, Solomianskyi, Holosiivskyi, Dniprovskyi and Darnytskyi districts were without power following the strikes.

Non-residential buildings were damaged in the Obolonskyi and Holosiivskyi districts, while transport and logistics infrastructure was hit in the Podilskyi and Darnytskyi districts, it said in a statement.
Why does Ukraine keep hitting Russia's prized Kerch Bridge?

Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a ballistic missile attack damaged the Podilskyi Bridge, forcing authorities to close traffic from the right bank to the left bank of the Dnipro River. The Darnitskyi Bridge was also damaged, he said.

A further strike hit the Southern Bridge, where traffic remains restricted. Only vehicles weighing up to 10 tons traveling from the left bank to the right bank, and public transport weighing up to 18 tons, are being permitted, he said.
Klitschko urged residents to avoid traveling into the city by private car unless absolutely necessary. He asked businesses and institutions to arrange remote working wherever possible.

articles.title: Lufthansa to cut 1,000 jobs, citing ongoing losses — reports
articles.summary: According to a letter obtained by the media, Lufthansa's executive board said the German company is losing €20 million every month. In addition to job cuts, operational cuts are also planned.

image.caption: Lufthansa is also the largest airline in Europe, in terms of passengers carriedImage: Ardan Fuessmann/Eibner-Pressefoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany's flagship airline Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs, according to a company letter seen by German news agency DPA and news outlets.
The letter was reportedly signed by Lufthansa CEO Jens Ritter and four other board members.
Why is Lufthansa cutting 1,000 jobs?
This is reportedly down to ongoing financial losses. In the first nine months of the year, the airline recorded an operating loss of €180 million ($197 million).
VW on the brink

The executive board said on average the loss amounts to €20 million every month, according to media reports. The board stated in the letter that "this is the third year in a row of not being financially successful."
"Lufthansa is currently not competitive in terms of its cost structure, efficiency and productivity," the letter said.
At the end of 2025, the Lufthansa group employed some 67,100 people, up 1% from the previous year.
How else is Lufthansa planning to save money?

The company also plans to cut employee travel benefits, restructure its hub operations to reduce crew overnight stays abroad, and reduce short- and medium-haul capacity by replacing some A320 aircraft with A220 jets.

Furthermore, it plans to equip ten aircraft per month with Starlink, a satellite internet service developed by tech billionaire Elon Musk. The airline hopes to generate "additional revenue” by monetizing onboard internet access, according to the letter.
The time frame of the cuts is unclear. It's also unknown whether the cuts were a part of a previously announced downsizing.
In September 2025, Lufthansa said it would slash 4,000 administrative positions due to the implementation of AI and digitalization.
In regards to this year, Lufthansa has faced rising fuel costs spurred by the US-Israeli war with Iran, further complicating its financial outlook.

articles.title: White House removes cyber-security chief after series of tech outages
articles.summary: CBS is reporting he has been fired after losing the confidence of White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.

blocks.text: The top cyber-security official in the US government is leaving his post after a string of tech outages which hit the National Security Agency (NSA), the US air traffic control system and some banks.
Sean Cairncross had been national cyber director since August 2025.
CBS, the BBC's US news partner, reported he had been fired, external after losing the confidence of White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio posted on X, external to say Department of Defense chief information officer Kirsten Davies was the new national cyber director.
The AFP news agency and CBS both said sources had told them Cairncross was fired, in a move supported by President Donald Trump.

The news, first reported by Axios, external, follows security concerns, including the ability of advanced AI models - mostly from US companies - to discover vulnerabilities which humans would not be able to find on their own.
Earlier this week, Rubio said there was "zero evidence" the outages were connected, adding "we are not under systemic attack".
But the fact that so many have happened in quick succession has left some people worried about the safety of the tech which is heavily relied on in all aspects of daily life.

articles.title: Jinggoy Estrada's 'fees' linked to Bulacan pumping stations, solar lights --witness
articles.summary: Senator Jinggoy Estrada"s P213 million worth of "commitment fees" or “kickbacks” stemmed from P355 million worth of pumping stations and P500 million worth of solar street lights in Bulacan, a…

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 5:34pm

Senator Jinggoy Estrada’s P213 million worth of "commitment fees" or “kickbacks” stemmed from P355 million worth of pumping stations and P500 million worth of solar street lights in Bulacan, a prosecution witness said Friday.

Carlo Rivera, a former engineer at the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Bulacan First District Engineering Office (DEO), gave testimony during the ongoing hearing on the bail petition filed by Estrada before the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division.
Estrada is facing a P573 million plunder charge over his alleged involvement in the flood control kickback scheme.

“Ang sabi po niya prepare a list for Senator Estrada…iyong P300 million pumping station, i-tag kay SJE,” Rivera said, referring to this former boss, state witness and ex-Bulacan First DEO District Engineer Henry Alcantara.
It was Alcantara who previously told the anti-graft court that Estrada got a 25% commitment fee per project. Alcantara, however, did not specify the nature of these Bulacan projects.
“The total amount of solar street lights is P500 million,” Rivera said.
Another prosecution witness, Edrick San Diego, said he served as a driver for Alcantara but was paid as a lot technician.
Likewise, San Diego said his task was only to deliver the boxes to state witness and the DPWH Undersecretary Roberto Bernardo, not to Estrada.
“Hindi ko alam ano nangyari [sa mga boxes] after madeliver sa Diamond Hotel,” San Diego said.
After San Diego’s testimony, the prosecution informed the Sandiganbayan that San Diego would be its last witness.
As a result, the Sandiganbayan gave the prosecution 10 days to submit its formal offer of evidence. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: [Pinoy Criminology] Killing of judges threatens the rule of law
articles.summary: A country that cannot protect its judges cannot promise its people a fair hearing, a just decision, or the rule of law

blocks.text: Another judge has fallen to assassins, and another court has been left to mourn. Judge Joseph Wee Sit, presiding over Branch 2 of the Regional Trial Court in Isabela City, Basilan, was shot dead in Zamboanga City on November 12. He was a young judge, only a little over a year into service on the bench, with his life and public service still opening before him.

This should outrage not only the legal profession, but the entire Filipino community. The killing is horrifying on its own, but it also carries a danger beyond one family’s grief. Every bullet fired at a judge is a threat to the institution that must decide disputes by law.

Whether this killing was intended to intimidate the judiciary remains for investigators to establish. But we cannot pretend an attack on a judge is merely a private crime, detached from public office. Judges sometimes confront politically charged, contested cases, where their decisions threaten interests powerful enough to answer law with force.

That possibility makes the killing all the more urgent to investigate, without prematurely declaring who ordered it or why. A murder can terrorize a court before its motive becomes known, because judges understand the warning implicit in violence.

The judiciary is supposed to be impartial and independent. Judges swear to decide cases on their merits, on the facts presented, and the law that governs them. They must be able to rule without fear or favor, even when their decisions anger the powerful or disappoint the public. When judges know that their lives, limbs, and careers are on the line, safety can begin to shape judgment. Then decisions are made not on merit, but on power; that is rule by men, not rule of law.

I have written about judgments arriving after 21 years, people trapped in judicial limbo, and detention prolonged by vacancies and delay. Those problems may look different from the murder of a judge, but they expose the same fragility. A court cannot guard liberty when it lacks time, personnel, and resources to hear cases fairly and promptly. Nor can the public trust justice when the law’s guardians are left vulnerable, unsupported, or pressured by political power. The judge should be the immediate guardian of liberty, and accountability separates justice from mere force.

That protection begins before a judge enters the courtroom. It begins with the appointment process, where judicial posts must never become prizes in partisan warfare. If lawyers must beg political patrons for judicial posts, obligations and loyalty tests can precede their first ruling. That is an unfair burden to place on young, idealistic lawyers, then send them to decide cases affecting the lives and fortunes of powerful people. Appointments must rest on merit alone, measured through integrity, ability, experience, and the courage to apply law equally.

The Judicial and Bar Council must be strengthened in its work of recruiting, selecting, and recommending judges and justices. Malacañang, as the final appointing authority, must respect the council’s merit-based recommendations and choose the most qualified candidates. That principle has too often remained aspirational, invoked in speeches but weakened by political calculation. An appointment system based on merit gives judges legitimacy and weakens patrons’ leverage over the bench. It also assures the public that judicial office is earned through qualification and service, rather than political loyalty.

We must also strengthen the judiciary after appointment. Congress and the presidency must provide more judges, court staff, functioning offices, and dependable operational budgets. Judges cannot deliver justice effectively when they lack the personnel, equipment, and basic resources to do their work. Courts should not have to depend on mayors, governors, or legislators for support that belongs to the national government. Local officials must respect independence, while the national government ensures judges never depend on local favor.

Protection must be real, sustained, and visible, especially for judges serving in places where cases carry exceptional risks. That means assessing threats, protecting court personnel, and coordinating security without letting security arrangements compromise judicial independence.

The investigation must establish who killed Judge Wee Sit, identify any instigators, and determine whether the attack was connected to his work. The Supreme Court has mobilized its judicial marshals to work with law enforcement, a necessary step toward accountability. The state must also stand with his family and every judge who returns to court despite danger.

Otherwise, judges will be reduced from instruments of law to instruments of the powerful. Disgruntled politicians, criminals, and businessmen will learn that terror can clear a judge from their path. Young lawyers attracted to public service will see that idealism can cost them their lives, while the state offers little protection.

That is how fear enters the courtroom, and how justice quietly yields to those who can threaten it. A country that cannot protect its judges cannot promise its people a fair hearing, a just decision, or the rule of law. – Rappler.com
Raymund E. Narag, PhD, is an associate professor in criminology and criminal justice at the School of Justice and Public Safety, Southern Illinois University, Carbondale.

articles.title: Defense witness: No reason for Cale88 income to go beyond P208M
articles.summary: The defense witness from the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte said Friday there was no reason for Cale88 Foods Corporation to surpass its…

blocks.text: FROM 2022 TO 2025
Published November 20, 2026 5:25pm

The defense witness from the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte said Friday there was no reason for Cale88 Foods Corporation to surpass its declared sales of P208 million during the years 2022 to 2025.

On Day 45 of the impeachment trial, Senator-judge and Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian asked DTI Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo about Cale88, the food company linked to Duterte's husband Manases Carpio.
"From 2022 to 2025, ang audited sales ng Cale88 is P208 million, tama po ba (is that correct)?" Gatchalian said, citing DTI documents.
"Opo (Yes), honorable judge," Rodolfo replied.
Gatchalian then presented data from the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC), which showed that Cale88 had an inflow of P776 million compared to an outflow of P154.611 million.

"Ang inward remittance is about P776 million… sa inyong karanasan, dahil alam ko na expert kayo pagdating sa incentives, matagal na rin kayo sa BOI (Board of Investments), ano 'yung possible reason dito dahil ang laki ng discrepancy? Mayroon bang undervaluing of sales, hindi nagdedeklera nang tama? Base sa inyong analysis," Gatchalian asked.

(The inward remittance is about P776 million… in your experience, because you are an expert when it comes to incentives, you have been with the BOI for a long time, what is the possible reason for the large discrepancy.)
Gatchalian added that based on a submitted balance sheet, there was also P20 million in advances from shareholders. Despite this, it would still not explain the large amount, he said.

"In relation po, Honorable Judge, doon sa operations po ng kumpanya at saka po doon sa sinubmit sa aming dokumento, wala ako ng makitang rason para tumaas po sila ng more than dito po sa declared sales revenue po nila na sinubmit sa amin," Rodolfo said.
(In relation, Honorable Judge, to the operations of the company and the submitted documents, I do not see a reason for this to go higher than the declared sales revenue that was submitted to us.)
The DTI also submitted bank certifications to the impeachment court, including one in 2023 indicating $352,000 in sales or about P22.48 million with the current exchange rate.
In 2025, there was another inflow of $368,000, or about P23.5 million.
Rodolfo said this amounted to $721,283 (about P46 million). The Senate President noted that this was still far from the amount found by the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC).
Last October, AMLC Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura testified said that Cale88 had aggregate transactions amounting to P1.25 billion from 2022 to 2025.
Buenaventura also said Cale88 received P319 million from China and Hong Kong, based on AMLC's covered transaction reports (CTRs) and suspicious transaction reports (STR).
Unavailed tax incentives
Meanwhile, Gatchalian also noted that Cale88 did not avail of any tax incentives from the BOI such as the income tax holiday (ITH).

"Why go through all the trouble tapos hindi ka rin mag-a-apply ng VAT zero rating? Sabi nga kanina ni former senate president Tito Sotto, pati other incentives like ITH, 'yung customs duty exemptions, bakit hindi sila nag-apply?" Gatchalian asked, referring to value-added tax.
(Why go through all the trouble and then not apply for VAT zero rating? Former senate president Tito Sotto pointed out that other incentives like the ITH, customs exemptions, why did they not apply?)
Rodolfo explained that given that Cale88 was export-oriented, the VAT zero rating was highly competitive.
"VAT zero rating 'yung isa sa mga pinag-aawayan. It has to be very facilitative. Within that context po, hindi ko rin alam kung bakit hindi siya nag-apply," Rodolfo said.
(The VAT zero rating is fought over. It has to be very facilitative. Within that context, I do not know why they did not apply.)
— VDV, GMA News

articles.title: California investigates Nvidia over whether chip exports ended up in China
articles.summary:
State attorney says scandal ‘raises bright red flags’ and aims to find out if company misled investors

California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that

blocks.text: California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.

Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based company’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.
“The conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” said Bonta.
“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors.”
The subpoena, issued on Thursday, followed Huang’s resignation a week ago after it emerged he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.

Alice Huang, who is not related, is associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which has bought nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) of Nvidia chips and hardware in recent years, and is being investigated for possibly diverting advanced restricted chips to China.
Megaspeed has said it is a “legitimate and lawful” business, and that Huang left the company late last year.
Bonta said the investigation would also look at whether the former Nvidia chief’s actions resulted in confidential information being passed to China.

“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information,” he said. “And if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law.”
after newsletter promotion
Nvidia’s shares are down by a fifth since Huang admitted the extramarital affair, hitting a one-year low at the close of trading on Thursday, and wiping almost $1tn off its market value.

Earlier this week, Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair, said the company had no intention of reinstating Huang after the former CEO said he would be “honoured” to return. Elon Musk and a host of tech bosses had campaigned for Nvidia to bring him back.
Huang is due to testify before several congressional committees over the potential breach of national security on 1 December.

articles.title: Have we missed our chance to stop climate change?
articles.summary: From record-breaking heat to devastating floods and wildfires, the warning signs are everywhere. Can rising temperatures still be brought under control?

image.caption: Has the world acted too late to stop catastrophic climate change?Image: Abriansyah Liberto/REUTERS

blocks.text: When world leaders agreed to do what they could to stop the world from overheating back in 2015, it was heralded as a victorious moment. Hope rippled from Paris, where the historic deal was made.

Since then, efforts to curb the use of planet-warming fossil fuels have achieved some success, with coal, oil and gas falling to a record low share of global primary energy supply. But they still account for around 86% of the world's energy.
"We're still burning stuff like [it's] the 19th century," Mark Maslin, professor of Earth System Science at University College London, told DW.

And that has consequences. The United Nations now says overshooting the temperature threshold agreed in Paris 11 years ago is inevitable. That means even more extreme weather events, like storms, flooding, droughts and deadly heat waves and resultant crop failures and water shortages across the world.

The impacts are already being felt globally. This summer, Europe alone recorded 50,000 heat-related deaths in urban areas. In Delhi, India, summer heat waves saw temperatures soar above 45 degrees Celsius (113 Fahrenheit). Even in the relative cool of the evening, there was little respite.
"It feels like your eyes are burning," said Disha Ravi co-founder of the India chapter of youth climate movement Fridays for Future (FFF). "I always describe it as being cooked alive in an oven."
Heat waves and other weather extremes are killing people now, says Ravi, and she is aware that as the global average temperature continues to rise, life is only set to become tougher.
"Even at this moment where we haven't even reached the worst of what it could be, it's already difficult," she said.
"We should have dealt with climate change 10, 20 years ago," Maslin said.
Shoulda, woulda, coulda: Is it too late to bring temperatures under control?
The UN now says that the world must keep the time it spends in overshoot as brief as possible, bringing global heating back down by the end of the century.

The longer the planet spends above the threshold, the greater the risk of triggering irreversible, self-perpetuating tipping points, such as massive forest die-back and permafrost melting that would release huge amounts of carbon into the atmosphere.

blocks.caption: As permafrost melts, it releases carbon dioxide which adds to the greenhouse gas effect that continues to warm the planetImage: MAXIM SHEMETOV/REUTERS

blocks.text: A recent report by science-based assessment Climate Action Tracker says limiting overshoot will require policies to rapidly and steeply reduce the emissions warping the climate.

"The stark choice for governments is to continue to support the fossil fuel industry, which would consign humanity to insurmountable economic damages, rising mortality from heat and climate-driven diseases and disasters that they are unable to adapt to — or pivot to the solutions which are available and cheaper than ever," the authors said.

Failure to cut emissions quickly has made it significantly harder to get climate change under control, and the window for doing so is rapidly closing. But Maslin refers to a Chinese proverb: "When is the best time to plant a tree? Yesterday. When's the next best time to plant a tree? Today."

He points to the massive expansion in renewable energy as reason not to despair. Wind, solar and hydropower accounted for around 34% of global electricity production in 2025 and are increasingly being used to meet rising demand.
Last year, record growth in solar power meant that clean energy met all new global electricity demand, stifling new fossil fuel generation, according to an analysis by energy think tank Ember.

blocks.caption: Solar energy has experienced record growth for years Image: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "At the moment, $2 trillion is being invested in new renewable energy projects around the world, which is twice as much as fossil fuels," Maslin said.
But no country is weaning itself off fossil fuels quickly enough to limit the time spent in overshoot. "The transition is happening, it's just not happening fast enough," he added.
The countries pushing for a fossil fuel phaseout

One of the problems is that most climate and energy plans focus on building a green energy system rather than creating policy to shift away from fossil fuel use and production, according to recent report on how to manage the transition by nonprofit research organization, World Resources Institute.
A group of 57 states is working together to manage and accelerate the complicated task of phasing out oil, coal and gas by creating specific roadmaps to do so.

Under the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels initiative (TAFF) initiative, Brazil has published a global roadmap that suggests various measures that can be tailored to each country's financial circumstances and capabilities.
So far, a small but growing number of countries, including, Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany, and Finland, have released national roadmaps.
COP31: Can electrification replace fossil fuels?

Yet renewables advocacy group Oil Change International says they largely repackage existing commitments rather than offering new ones, when "what we need is an accelerated timeline for a clean, secure energy system."

France is sticking to a previously announced deadline of phasing out fossil fuels entirely by 2050. The Netherlands has not published binding dates for quitting oil and gas, and will continue to extract gas in the North Sea.

Germany, however, explicitly mentioned transitioning away from fossil fuels by 2045 for the first time, in line with its existing climate neutrality target. The country has also reduced its emissions by 48% compared to 1990 levels.

And while Finland has not set a hard and fast target for phasing out the fossil fuels that still account for 26% of its total energy consumption, it already generates more than 96% of electricity from non-fossil sources.

"None of these examples is a perfect template," according to the WRI report. "But together, they show that countries are already developing many of the core ingredients of a fossil fuel transition plan."
Every fraction of a degree matters
Limiting the time spent in overshoot would mean fossil fuel use falling 20% by 2030 and being phased out completely by 2070, according to research institute Climate Analytics.
It also means removing hundreds of billions of tons of CO2 from the atmosphere using carbon removal technologies that remain unproven at scale, as well as nature-based approaches like reforestation.
And it requires fast action on the short-lived but highly potent greenhouse gas methane. A 45% cut would reduce warming by 0.3%, according to the UN.

blocks.caption: Each fraction of a degree of warming will bring with it escalating climate extremes so it's still all to play for, say scientistsImage: Apu Gomes/AFP

blocks.text: Scientists stress that every fraction of a degree matters as the world blows past the threshold of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) of warming above pre-industrial levels. That's because every increment will bring more extreme heat, heavier rainfall, rising seas, and greater and more catastrophic risk for everyone around the world.
Still, even in the face of accelerating climate change, FFF co-founder Ravi rejects the idea that it is too late to act.
"I refuse to believe we'll ever run out of time. No matter how bad it gets," she said. "We owe it to ourselves. We owe it to each other to always try to get out of this mess."

articles.title: California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state
articles.summary:
Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded

Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive…

blocks.text: Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.

Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.

blocks.caption: A large wave pours over the seawall in Pacifica. Photograph: Fred Greaves/Reuters
