articles.title: Andy Burnham heads to Brussels as UK and EU close in on Brexit reset deal – live
articles.summary:
UK and EU have provisionally agreed to allow 100,000 EU citizens to come to the UK every year under a new mobility scheme.

Senior correspondent

France’s insistence…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 2m agoUK and EU plan first talks on sending refused asylum seekers to third countries
10m agoRow over voting rights dispels myths that UK comes to negotiations from position of strength - snap analysis
16m agoTalks went down to the wire this morning
17m agoMorning opening: Second post-Brexit EU-UK summit gets under way in Brussels

blocks.text: UK and EU plan first talks on sending refused asylum seekers to third countries
Rajeev Syal and Lisa O’Carroll
The UK and the EU plan to establish formal talks for the first time about sending rejected asylum seekers to third-country hubs, according to a leaked document.

blocks.caption: A migrant leaves an abandoned warehouse, where some migrants are taking shelter during the winter months, in Marck, near Calais, northern France. Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: A draft of a joint statement expected to be signed by Andy Burnham and Ursula von der Leyen at a summit on Friday morning states that both sides will establish “a structured dialogue” to discuss “returns to third countries”.
Until now, the Home Office has been seeking bilateral agreements with third countries allowing the removal of migrants, but with no obvious success.
Last week, five EU countries – Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands – announced an agreement in principle with Rwanda to establish a migrant “return hub” there in 2027.

Burnham hinted at possible cooperation with EU countries last week when he told reporters that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that [the five-country deal] with interest, learning from what went on in the past”. He said: “The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”
The UK has been fighting for deeper cooperation with the EU on migration, with the new deal on a “strategic dialogue” secured in the last two weeks by negotiators in Brussels.

It is a key part of the UK-EU reset pact, which also covers a youth mobility scheme, tariffs on Chinese imports, food and drink exports to the EU and a wider restatement of commitment on defence and security.
Informed sources confirmed this was the first time the UK and the EU had agreed to “open a dialogue on returns” after the launch of the bloc’s Channel action plan in June this year.
Whitehall sources said the UK was now open to the possibility of sending rejected claimants to Rwanda – a recent pivot from the position under Keir Starmer’s government, which rejected the move.
According to a draft of the joint agreement, negotiations over third-country hubs will be part of increased cooperation to tackle irregular migration.
Row over voting rights dispels myths that UK comes to negotiations from position of strength - snap analysis

blocks.caption: Lisa O’Carroll

blocks.text: Lisa O’Carroll
Senior correspondent

France’s insistence that the UK could not have voting rights at any stage during the shaping of legislation on food standards and public health risks relating to food and agri products is a line in the sand for Andy Burnham.

blocks.caption: Journalists arrive as preparations are made for the EU-UK Summit at the European Council building in Brussels. Photograph: Virginia Mayo/AP

blocks.text: The last night tensions at the ambassadors meeting will be a sharp lesson for anyone in the UK who clings to the idea that negotiating with the EU comes from a position of strength: the UK is not a member of the EU and despite the warm feelings to the Labour government in European capitals, benefits of the club are not extended to non members.
It also underlines the feeling expressed by several large member states this week that the way forward after this summit is not more iterative reset summits or mini-deals.

Yes, there will be negotiations on allowing the UK into the energy single market as this is in the joint interests of both sides in the wake of the Ukraine war. But no talks on pharma or chemicals, according to some capitals.
As one diplomat said:
“It puts down a marker warning the UK that cherry picking bits of the single market mean you are a rule taker.”
“It makes the choice for Britain starker and more binary” and shows that “the alternatives are basically muddling along with a version of the status quo or rejoining,” they said.

blocks.caption: Jennifer Rankin

blocks.text: Jennifer Rankin
in Brussels
UK prime minister Andy Burnham will be welcomed with a rendition of God Save the King and the Ode to Joy when he attends the opening ceremony around 10.30am local time.

blocks.caption: Musicians rehearse the British national anthem and the European anthem ahead of the EU-UK summit in Brussels, Belgium. Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPA

blocks.text: Talks went down to the wire this morning
Talks to seal today’s reset in relations between the UK and the EU went write down to the wire this morning.
In what is known as a “silence procedure”, the EU issued a late night compromise text to all member states after a meeting of crunch hours long meeting of ambassadors in Brussels last night.
Under the procedure if no member states breaks the silence the text is considered “adopted” and would then be made available for signing by the UK – bar any last minute hitches on its side.
This morning diplomats said “no one had broken the silence”. The headline agreements are:

items: Food and drink deal, setting up sanitary and phyto sanitary common area
An electricity carbon emissions deal
Cap of 100,000 EU citizens under 31 years old to come to the UK under a new youth mobility scheme
The issue of tuition fees kicked down the road - a supplementary agreement has been reached to sort this out within the next six months
This allows the UK to hold up the youth deal if the EU does not give it what it needs in the Made in Europe legislation which is expected to reach its final negotiations stages by Easter too.

No voting rights for the UK when the EU comes to writing new laws about food standards; this was never a realistic option as the UK is not a member of the EU, but the French led the resistance as the UK pushed for it equally as hard, instead the UK will be consullted at key stages
Industry groups say that must mean UK regulators are in the room at the early stages. Food regulation is very technical, the say and this is where the real decisions are taken.
The two sides will also open talks on UK entering the energy single market.

blocks.text: Morning opening: Second post-Brexit EU-UK summit gets under way in Brussels

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
The EU and UK will hold a long-awaited summit in Brussels on Friday – the second since Brexit – to hammer out the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc.

blocks.caption: A member of protocol arranges the Union flag and EU flag as preparations are made for the EU-UK Summit at the European Council building in Brussels. Photograph: Virginia Mayo/AP

blocks.text: It will be attended by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and the president of the European Council, António Costa.
As our Brussels correspondent, Jennifer Rankin, explained:

“The two sides hope to announce three deals, which were initiated under Starmer’s government. First, a food and drink agreement that will remove a lot of Brexit red tape on animal and plant products, making it easier to trade meats, cheese, wine and flowers. To secure the deal, which is not expected to take effect until 2028, the UK will align with EU standards, meaning the government, for example, must abandon a planned ban on foie gras imports. A second agreement will link the British emissions trading system with its bigger EU cousin, restoring a link severed by Brexit. It is a significant step for industry because EU and UK businesses will be exempt from each other’s charges on high-carbon imports such as steel, cement and electricity. This agreement also requires alignment with relevant EU rules. The third deal has proved the most contentious: a youth mobility scheme that will give those aged 18-31 the right to live, work, travel and study on both sides of the Channel for up to three years. The scheme may not be up and running until 2030 – which is bad news for anyone in their late 20s.”
The leaders are expected to arrive 9.30am GMT (10.30am Brussels time), with “the leaders’ meeting” between Burnham, von der Leyen and Costa to follow.

A plenary session with UK ministers and EU commissioners is expected at 10.45am GMT (11.45am Brussels), and if all goes well we should then see the leaders tell us what they agreed around half past midday (1.30pm Brussels time).
I will bring you every single detail of the day here today. You won’t miss a thing.
It’s Friday, 20 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

blocks.text: Here is a roundup of headlines from India from Friday, November 20:
Pakistan's Climate Change Minister Musadik Malik arrived in New Delhi on Friday for a Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) cultural forum.

It is the first visit to India by a Pakistani federal minister since Bilawal Bhutto Zardari attended the SCO meeting in Goa in May 2023, and the first since last year's conflict between the two countries.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi is set to inaugurate the Civilizational Dialogue Forum, which runs from November 20 to 22. India invited Pakistan's culture minister in October, but Islamabad sent Malik instead.
Pakistan's Foreign Office said he would present the country's views on dialogue among civilizations and meet other SCO members on the sidelines, local media reported.
Malik said the visit is not a bilateral negotiation, according to NDTV. No breakthrough in frigid relations is expected.

The visit comes after the four-day India-Pakistan conflict of 2025, set off by the Pahalgam attack, which killed at least 70 people on both sides, AFP stated. It also comes two days after Indian forces killed Lashkar-e-Taiba commander Lateef Bhat.
Kashmir tourism struggles post Pahalgam attack
Opposition leaders criticized the government's move to host Malik.

"BJP always says that talks and terrorism cannot happen at the same time. But now, a Pakistani minister is visiting India for the SCO meeting," said Samajwadi Party leader Fakhrul Hasan Chand, NDTV reported.
Congress Member of Parliament Pramod Tiwari also recalled Malik's earlier remarks on the Indus Waters Treaty, calling his language that of a "terrorist," according to NDTV.
Earlier this year, Malik, referring to the Indus Waters Treaty suspension after last year's Pahalgam terror attack, had warned against "water aggression," pressing India to respect the 1960 treaty.
"Whoever touches our water, their hands would be cut off," he said at the time.

articles.title: Climbing up a Pangasinan hill, in the dark, to hear Rina’s story
articles.summary: Upper middle income? Our field work in Pangasinan is proof that statistics cannot tell us what it feels like to live in a house without electricity

blocks.text: “Neighbors” is Rappler People section’s space for community and human interest stories told in a personal way.

PANGASINAN, Philippines – There are moments during the field work with University of Santo Tomas (UST) student researchers that made me stop and think about the lack of social justice in this part of the world. This is a story about one of those moments.

We agreed not to film the encounter that I am about to narrate regardless of how tempting it was to capture the drama of the situation. Lest you forget, we are researchers, not content creators. We are after the truth, not validation.

The scene I am referring to is that of Gabrielle (interviewer) and Rina (interviewee). Please note that I am not using the real name of the respondent to protect her privacy. The women are about the same age, but they were born in two separate social classes.

Gabrielle is studying at UST, whereas Rina was forced to stop schooling to prioritize her work as a canteen staff in Urdaneta City. Gabrielle is busy chasing her dreams, studying culinary arts in the oldest existing university in Asia with the help of some of the country’s best academicians. Meanwhile, Rina is busy trying to survive. She works so that she could help feed her mom, dad, and siblings.

If Gabrielle is reaching for her brightest stars, Rina only wants to survive. In this economy, Rina surely knows how to be realistic. Maybe her only prayer right now is to have electricity in their house one day. “Kung nakaluwag-luwag (once we can afford it),” as old people say. The sight was heart-wrenching, to say the least.

On October 3, we made our way up the hill to Rina’s house, where her family lives. By the time we arrived, the sun was already giving way to darkness. The family cannot afford electricity, so darkness is simply not the absence of light inside their house. It is part of their everyday life. At night, the family has only the stars and a few solar-powered lights to illuminate their home. Using Rina’s surroundings as a backdrop, you can almost hear Coldplay’s “Yellow” or Joey Ayala’s “Buwan, Buwan” playing.

We interviewed the family after sunset. We watched as darkness slowly enveloped the house, as insects and animals began announcing their presence nearby. Perhaps, they are nature’s natural sensors, knowing the arrival of strangers. Their sounds may mean welcome. Or threat.

The transition from day to night has a strange effect on someone’s psyche when you are in the wild, especially in unfamiliar terrain. As a probinsiyano (man from the province), I found it strangely comforting. For my five companions, however, it was a different story. They came from the brightest metropolis in the country. I could sense how tense they were throughout the entire ordeal.

Pero, in fairness, hindi nagpatinag ang mga estudiyante ng USTe. Dala-dala nila ang mga flashlights ng kani-kanilang iPhone para suungin ang dilim. Nagmukha kaming mga gamu-gamo sa tuktok ng napakadilim na munting burol. Napakatapang pa rin ng mga researchers sa kabila ng ‘di pangkaraniwang kaba na hirap din nilang itago. Takot na takot sila, pero sumulong at tumuloy pa rin.

(To be fair to the UST students [I accompanied], they were not discouraged. The held their iPhones’ flashlights through the dark. We looked like fireflies atop a really dark hill. The researchers braved the way, despite the fear they tried hard to hide. They were so afraid, yet they soldiered on.)
Your professors must be so proud of you, mga kapatid (brothers and sisters). Go, USTe!

Anyway, the next house with a television and WiFi was almost a kilometer away from Rina’s house. To be honest, the house where we conducted our field work was quite literally in the middle of nowhere. The scene looked like something from the 1970s, during the heydays of FPJ Productions. It was the setting that could easily be made romantic and cinematic on film. But life taught me that some things are only romantic when you are watching them from a safe distance. In reality, the place was malamok (mosquito-infested). It was mainit (hot) even at nighttime. And it was quite creepy.

During the entire interview, I couldn’t stop thinking about the insanity of it all. Only last July, our President Bongbong Marcos bragged that the country had achieved the upper-middle-income status after nearly four decades. I do not doubt the statistics. What I doubt is whether the statistics tell the whole story. Because whatever this achievement means to the country, it means very little to the people I encountered during our field work.

Ilang taon ko na ring sinusundan ang kuwento ng mga tao sa likod ng tradisyong panagliyab, pero mas tumatanda lang sila at mas nangayayat. Ang pag-asenso ay napakamailap pa rin sa kanila kahit pa nagpapakahirap sila araw-araw at gabi-gabi.

(For years, I have been following the story of the people behind the panagliyab tradition. They are getting older, and thinner. Having a comfortable life remains elusive for them although they work hard day and night.)
(According to Lokalpedia, panagliyab is the tradition of “processing the sap of the silag, or buri palm.”)

Kung kailan pa tayo nagkaroon ng upper-middle-income status — whatever that means — ‘tsaka naman naging mas kalunos-lunos ang kalagayan ng mga managliyab na nakilala ko. Mas mahina na ngayon si Laki Berting na 78 anyos na. Hindi ko na rin mahanap ang mga ibang aking nakapanayam noong 2024. Hindi ko na alam kung buhay pa ba silang lahat.

(When we finally achieved the upper-middle-income status — whatever that means — that’s when the living conditions of the traditional artisans that I met more deplorable. Laki Berting, who is 78, has grown weaker. I can’t find anymore those I interviewed in 2024. I don’t even know if they are still alive.)

Lagi nating naririnig sa balita na gumaganda naman daw ang ekonomiya, pero bakit tila dumarami pa rin ang katulad ni Rina? Bakit kailangan pa ring umakyat sa puno ng mga silag ang isang 78-anyos na lolo para lamang manatiling buhay? Gusto lang naman daw niyang tulungan ang kanyang mga apo na ulila na sa ama. Upper-middle-income na nga ba talaga tayo? Bakit parang ang mahal pa ring mabuhay sa Pilipinas? Minsan, nakakapagod na ring magtanong nang magtanong. Wala rin kasing malinaw na sagot. Basta, ang mahalaga ay upper-middle-income na raw tayo.

(We often hear in the news that our economy is improving, but why does it seem that there are more people like Rina? Why does a 78-year-old grandfather have to climb up buri palm trees just to earn a living? He said he just wanted to support his grandchildren who had lost their father. Are we really an upper-middle-income country? Why does it feel like it’s difficult to survive in the Philippines? Sometimes, I get tired of asking questions. There are no clear answers anyway. The government just insists, we’re upper-middle-income.)

Mas madali na lang talagang mahalin ang ating kapwa-tao. Sa dulo naman ay tayo-tayo rin lang ang magtutulungan. Silver lining na lang maituturing na may mga tulad nina Gabrielle, Francine, Jaime, Kath, at Phia na handang tumapak sa putikan at literal na umakyat sa madilim na burol para kumalap ng mga datos upang maging batayan ng katotohanang ibabahagi nila sa Maynila. Napakahusay ng mga magulang at guro na nagpalaki sa mga batang mananaliksik na aking sinamahan sa loob ng dalawang araw. Lumaki po sila nang napakaayos at napakarangal. Mapalad lang din ako at nakilala ko sila.

(What’s easier to do is to love our fellowmen. In the end, we’ve only got each other to help. I consider it a silver lining that there are students like Gabrielle, Francine, Jaime, Kath, and Phia who were willing to walk in the mud and climb up a dark hill to gather data on which they would base the truth that they would share in Manila. I admire the parents and teachers who raised these young researchers whom I guided for two days. They grew up decent and honorable. I’m blessed I got to know them.)

At the end of the day, these young researchers sought the welfare of the managliyab. They showed us that helping them and preserving the tradition should be an ultimate priority because a tradition cannot survive if we do not value the people who carry it. May panagliyab live on despite the increasing challenges.

I pray that researchers will not get tired of listening to the stories of people from the lowest ranks of the social ladder. Especially today, when the statistics serves as the sole basis of all the official pronouncements, it does not help to be so gullible. Statistics can tell us that the economy is growing, that the country has moved up another rung on the economic ladder, and that we are now upper-middle-income.

But statistics cannot tell us what it feels like to live in a house without electricity, and they certainly cannot tell us whether people like Rina feel that the country is progressing. Sometimes, these figures are seemingly out of touch, misleading, and simply fail to capture the truth. Hence, we need to engage with one another more than ever before to find the truth for ourselves. And sometimes, the only way to find the truth is to climb that dark mountain ourselves. – Rappler.com
Julius B. Cayabyab is an instructor at Pangasinan State University. His work in higher education informs his perspectives on issues concerning education, society, culture, and community development.

articles.title: Sara Duterte's tree planting 'connection' with Calle88 questioned in impeachment trial
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel raised questions Friday regarding the alleged possible connection of Vice President Sara Duterte's tree planting activities with Cale88 Foods Corporation.

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 4:11pm
The House prosecution panel raised questions Friday regarding the alleged possible connection of Vice President Sara Duterte's tree planting activities with Cale88 Foods Corporation.

Cale88, the food firm linked to Duterte's husband Manases Carpio, has come under scrutiny during the vice president's impeachment trial over its profits earned with only two employees and its supposed financial inflows from China.
During the cross examination of Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo on Day 45 of the trial, private prosecutor Erwin Matib flashed photos of Duterte planting trees.
The defense counsel initially objected on the basis of relevance, but Presiding Officer Francis Escudero allowed Matib to continue, granted that he is on a short leash.

"Tama po ba na itong pagtatanim ng mga puno ni Vice President Sara Duterte ay connected sa pag-comply ng Cale88 Foods sa tree planting activities na requirement ng Board of Investment? In fact, ang requirement ng Board of Investment ay magtanim dapat ang enterprises ng at least 100 forest trees. May ganoong requirement, tama po ba?" Matib said.

(Is it correct that Vice President Sara Duterte tree planting is connected with with Cale88's compliance with the tree planting requirements of the Board of Investment? In fact, the requirement of the Board of Investment is to plant at least 100 forest trees. There is a requirement for this, right?)
Before Rodolfo could answer, defense counsel Justin Gular objected.

"Objection, your honor, misleading. There is no prior testimony coming from the witness wherein he testified that the vice president participated in the compliance requirement of tree planting," Gullar said.

"The insinuation being made by the prosecution that the pictures being shown or that was displayed of the vice president planting trees had any relation to Cale88 Foods Corporation's registration is misleading, malicious and callous, your honor," he added.
Escudero sustained Gular's objection, telling Matib to carry on to the next point.
Rodolfo affirmed that tree planting was part of Board of Investment's (BOI) requirements. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Defense witness: Cale88 has zero employees in 2024, two in 2025
articles.summary: Cale88 Foods Corporation, a listed business interest of Vice President Sara Duterte"s husband, Manases Carpio, in their joint wealth statement, recorded zero employees in 2024 and two employees in…

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 4:08pm

Cale88 Foods Corporation, a listed business interest of Vice President Sara Duterte’s husband, Manases Carpio, in their joint wealth statement, recorded zero employees in 2024 and two employees in 2025, a defense witness said Friday.

Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo of DTI’s Industry Development and Investment Promotions Group made the testimony during the cross-examination of private prosecutor Erwin Matib wherein the witness was confronted with General Information Sheet (GIS) submitted by Cale88 to the Board of Investments (BOI).

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero allowed the prosecution to confront Rodolfo, who also serves as the BOI’s Managing Head, with Cale88 Foods Corp. GIS for years 2024 and 2025 because he was familiar with such documents. Cale88 Foods Corp. changed ownership to Pikimong Pikimong Philippines Corp.
Asked by Matib how many rank-and-file employees Cale88 Foods Corp. had in 2024 based on GIS, Rodolfo said, “Wala po.” (None.)
Matib then asked Rodolfo if Cale88 Foods Corp. had a manpower complement in 2024 based on GIS, to which Rodolfo replied, “Wala rin po.” (There’s also none.)
Likewise, Rodolfo said he did not see any Cale88 Foods Corp. submission on its employees’ Social Security System and PhilHealth benefits.
He also explained that the BOI would not readily know the list of employees of a business entity unless the company applies for an incentive before the BOI.
“Ang pangbangga kasi namin iyong incentives. Pag nag-avail po sila ng incentive, hihingin po namin ‘yun (list of employees),” Rodolfo said.
(We base it on the incentives. If a firm seeks an incentive, we’ll ask for a list of incentives.)
“Dahil hindi naman siya nag-avail na incentive, wala pong pang bangga ho,” Rodolfo added.
(Because they did not avail of an incentive, we won’t have that record [of employees].)

Rodolfo earlier said during the same impeachment proceedings that based on Cale88 Foods Corp.’s BOI form submissions, its number of employees was reduced from 201 in 2024 to 50 in 2025 because of the change in ownership.

Lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro of Batangas, in a separate interview, noted that such a discrepancy in Cale88 Foods Corp. submissions proves that the testimony of the prosecution witness and CPA-lawyer Alex Cabrera is an implausible business model.

“We saw the inconsistency [in submitted documents]. When you say it is an implausible business model, it does not necessarily mean a zero operation. We have to read that terminology on the basis of the entire procedure of the expert witness. For me, the fact that BIR documents (GIS) do not tally with the data with BOI makes it an implausible business model already,” Luistro told reporters.

“Because we need to be very consistent on the business data that we are submitting to the government agencies such as the DTI, Securities and Exchange Commission, and take note of the inward remittances reported by the AMLC (Anti-Money Laundering Council). Implausible is a very general term, and it could mean as well that inconsistent data or information which are being submitted or at the very least shown by the different government agencies,” Luistro added.

Defense witness and AML Consulting PH head, Atty. Rainer Dela Fuente, earlier testified that there were red flags in Cale88 Foods Corporation operations given that the firm only has two employees, received P319 million remittances from China and recorded 757 covered transactions and suspicious transactions worth P1.2 billion based on AMLC records.
Dela Fuente, however, said such red flags are not automatically illegal. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Marcos signs law expanding vouchers to kindergarten, elementary students
articles.summary: The law, known as the Basic Education Voucher Assistance Act, provides financial assistance to students in areas with “congested” public schools, or schools where enrollment exceeds…

blocks.text: November 20, 2026 | 4:08pm
This photo taken on March 21, 2025, shows students doing colouring activities at an elementary school at Baseco in Manila.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — Kindergarten and elementary students may avail of the government's basic education voucher program beginning in the 2027-2028 school year, following President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.'s signing of Republic Act 12327 on Friday, November 20.

The law, known as the Basic Education Voucher Assistance Act, provides financial assistance to students in areas with “congested” public schools, or schools where enrollment exceeds classroom capacity, so they may enroll in accredited private schools.
Students in areas where there are no public schools or no public schools offering subjects and electives aligned with their chosen senior high school pathways are also eligible for the vouchers.
The financial aid will be made available to learners belonging to middle-middle-income households and below.
Middle-middle-income households are those with a monthly income ranging from P55,492 to P97,111, according to the Philippine Institute for Development Studies.
Under the law, participating private schools may receive teacher training and salary subsidies.

Schools, however, are not allowed to restrict a student's participation due to delayed reimbursement of the voucher and may be barred from participating in other programs under the Department of Education if found at fault.

The Bureau of Private Education, established within DepEd under the law, will implement the voucher program, enforce regulatory requirements for private schools and help implement other efforts to decongest public schools.

articles.title: Senior Tories urge Badenoch to drop Brexit talk in major strategy shift, sources say
articles.summary: Exclusive: While PM pushes for EU reset, Tory leader is moving away from ‘divisive’ issue that defined party for years

blocks.text: Kemi Badenoch has been advised by her team to limit the amount of time she spends discussing Brexit and Europe, the Guardian has been told, moving the Conservatives away from an issue that defined the party for many years.

While the Tory leader still gives views on Brexit – in an opinion piece in the Daily Mail on Thursday she condemned Andy Burnham’s ongoing reset with the EU as a “backwards” move – sources say it is now seen as a second-order subject.
Instead, Badenoch intends to focus on areas the party believes are more fertile electoral ground, in particular the economy, the cost of social security and defence.

One source said Badenoch had been advised to shift the narrative away from Brexit by Stephen Gilbert, a former Conservative official who is now a peer and who joined the Tory leader’s team as a senior political adviser a year ago.
Although another party source said Gilbert’s advice was “more nuanced” than this, Badenoch’s recent run of speeches and interventions appears to demonstrate the change.

In eight sets of prime minister’s questions since Burnham entered No 10 over the summer, Badenoch and her deputy, Alex Burghart, who took one session when Burnham was away, have focused on Europe just once, on 28 October, when she challenged the PM on whether or not he wanted a new Brexit referendum.

Every other outing has focused on various aspects of the welfare state, the cost of living, or defence, also including subjects such as the budget, debt and whether or not the UK should drill for more North Sea oil and gas.

“The way I see it, this is less of a conscious attempt to sideline Europe than it is a way to talk more about the subjects we think are our strong points, like the economy and defence,” one senior Conservative said.

One Tory shadow minister said the wider party was firmly behind the idea: “Europe does still come up from time to time, but as a former remainer even I think we should move on. I’m not sure what is likely to change by us talking about it all the time.”
Another shadow minister said: “We don’t want to be talking about Brexit for multiple reasons – including the simple one that it was so awfully divisive.”

Badenoch does still at times defend Brexit to selected audiences, for example in Thursday’s Daily Mail piece, where she disputed Burnham’s charge that it had hampered the UK’s economic growth, saying the prime minister “wants to reopen arguments from 2016 because he has no answers for the world as it is”.

At other times her language on links with the EU has been more nuanced than the period when the Conservatives liked to disparage the continent as economically moribund and less relevant than more distant economies.

Asked about Burnham’s attempt to renegotiate the post-Brexit trade agreement during a press conference on defence earlier this month, Badenoch said: “They say they want to end red tape on food checks – that’s a good thing”, while then predicting this would not actually happen.

Badenoch also said she accepted that the deal with the EU could and should be updated: “The free trade agreement that we have with the EU, like many others, is one that needs constant negotiating. So I want to see Labour negotiating and improving on deals with all countries. That’s what you do when you have your own trade policy.”

A Conservative spokesperson said: “As Kemi has said, the last thing the country needs is to be dragged back into a debate on Brexit. That absolutely does not mean Kemi and the Conservatives won’t discuss the EU, but we will be very clear that Andy Burnham is only trying to reopen old wounds on Brexit because he doesn’t have anything to say about the challenges facing the country.
“Bringing down the welfare bill, funding defence, cutting taxes to promote growth can all be done outside the EU. Burnham’s reset is one big distraction and we will never shy away from saying so.”

articles.title: Voucher program now covers kinder to Grade 12 under new law
articles.summary: The voucher assistance program for private kindergarten and elementary schools is targeted for rollout in the 2027-2028 school year, subject to funding availability

blocks.text: CLASS ONGOING. Students of Santolan Elementary School in Pasig City attend class on August 12, 2026.
Jelo Ritzhie Mantaring/Rappler
The voucher assistance program for private kindergarten and elementary schools is targeted for rollout in the 2027-2028 school year, subject to funding availability

items: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed Republic Act No. 12327, expanding the government's voucher program for basic education to include kindergarten and elementary students from low-income households.

The law aims to alleviate congestion in public schools by prioritizing students from overcrowded institutions and areas without nearby public schools, with a target rollout for the program in the 2027-2028 school year.

The Department of Education will implement measures to prevent fraud in the program and establish an online portal for mapping classroom congestion, while also creating the Bureau of Private Education.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has signed a law that expanded the coverage of the government’s voucher program for basic education, which allows poor students to study in private schools.

Republic Act No. 12327 or the Basic Education Voucher Assistance Act — approved on November 12 and publicized on Friday, November 20 — aims to decongest public schools in the country. (READ: [OPINION] There’s a bigger problem than the classroom shortage — school congestion)

The measure, which is among the Marcos administration’s priorities, broadened the Expanded Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education (E-GATSPE) Act, to include kindergarten and elementary school.
Currently, the decades-old E-GASTPE Act only provides tuition aid to students in private junior and senior high schools (SHS).
The target rollout for the voucher program of kindergarten to elementary is during the school year 2027-2028, subject to funding availability.
With the new law, students coming from congested public schools and multi-shift institutions, as well those living in areas without nearby public schools, will be prioritized for the voucher program.
The measure provides that beneficiaries from poor and low-income households receive a higher voucher amount.

It allows supplemental assistance by a top-up or co-fund aid from local governments, private sponsors, or other scholarship providers to cover the difference between the voucher amount and the total cost of schooling.
“Families will be empowered through a public registry detailing nearby participating private schools, slots, and fees,” read a part of the Department of Education (DepEd) statement.

“Importantly, the law protects learners by prohibiting schools from withholding records due to delayed government payments, penalizes fraudulent claims, and provides salary subsidies and training for private school teachers,” it added.

The DepEd faced the issue of “ghost students” in the SHS voucher program in 2025. In July 2026, the agency said a regional trial court had sentenced an individual to up to 14 years in prison for attempting to defraud the government program by submitting falsified documents.
But state auditors found that there were 58 “unverifiable” beneficiaries of the SHS voucher program, which resulted in an overpayment of P938,000 during the 2025-2026 school year.

In responding to that Commission on Audit report in September, the DepEd said it had “tightened beneficiary validation, billing, refund, and accountability measures” in the revised E-GATSPE guidelines released in April.
The DepEd said it would “continue to pursue accountability and the recovery of government funds where warranted.”
The agency is directed to establish an online portal for a nationwide mapping of classroom congestion, and annually update a decongestion framework to guide school prioritization.
The Bureau of Private Education would also be created under the DepEd.
Within three years, the DepEd should report to Congress whether congestion in public schools is addressed and learning outcomes of disadvantaged students are improved, among others. – Rappler.com

articles.title: China's Xi praises 'turnaround' in relationship with Australia
articles.summary: The leaders of Australia and China have held talks on sidelines of APEC summit. Australian PM Anthony Albanese is also slated to meet Chinese Premier Li Qiang.

image.caption: China's Xi also called for enhancing cooperation with Australia in agriculture, ​energy, the ‌green economy and artificial intelligenceImage: Lintao Zhang/Getty Images/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Chinese President Xi Jinping held talks on Friday, following which Xi hailed a "comprehensive turnaround" in the ties between two nations and Albanese said his country was engaging "constructively" with Beijing.
The leaders met on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Forum (APEC) summit in China's Shenzhen.
What did Xi say to Albanese?
Xi pointed out to Albanese that they had met four times since the latter became Australia's Prime Minister in 2022.
"I think it is fair to say that together we have brought about a comprehensive ​turnaround in China-Australia relations," the Chinese President said.
Xi also called for enhancing cooperation in agriculture, ​energy, the ‌green economy and artificial intelligence, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported.
Why is China important for Australia?
China is Australia's top trading partner.
The relations between the two countries hit rock bottom under Canberra's former centre-right coalition government, which had called for an independent inquiry into the origins of the coronavirus.
An angry China retaliated by imposing import curbs worth $13 billion (€12.2 billion) on Australian timber, coal, barley, lobsters and wine.
Since Albanese's centre-left Labor party came to power, China has lifted most of its blocks on Australian exports.

But friction in ties has surfaced occasionally on issues such as China conducting a missile test in the South Pacific and Australia tightening a foreign investment screening in the critical minerals sector.
"It is important that Australia continue to engage in a constructive way with China, manage our differences, but not be defined by them," Albanese told the media on Friday.
"What happens in China does matter for Australia," he added.
Iron ore, a pressure point
Albanese is expected to travel to Beijing and meet China's Premier Li Qiang later on Friday.

On Monday, Australia, which is the world's biggest producer of iron ore, called out China's "manipulation" of trade in the commodity over Beijing's formation of a central buying body to purchase ‌ore on behalf of its steelmakers.
A single buyer has increased bargaining power in negotiations with sellers.
Albanese and Li will attend a business roundtable comprising of senior executives from Australian mining giants Rio Tinto and BHP and ​Chinese company executives.

articles.title: Sara Duterte spokesman invokes free speech amid impeachment court's show-cause order
articles.summary: Lawyer Paolo Panelo, spokesperson of Vice President Sara Duterte, on Friday invoked the constitutional right to free speech following the Senate impeachment court's issuance of a show cause order…

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 3:28pm

Lawyer Paolo Panelo, spokesperson of Vice President Sara Duterte, on Friday invoked the constitutional right to free speech following the Senate impeachment court's issuance of a show cause order against him.
Earlier, Panelo made a comment that some senator-judges were acting as prosecutors.
In a statement, Panelo cited Supreme Court rulings recognizing the right of citizens to scrutinize and criticize public officials, including members of the judiciary.
He quoted the 2012 Supreme Court ruling in Garcia, Jr. v. Manrique, which stated that the power to punish for contempt does not place courts beyond public scrutiny or legitimate criticism.

Panelo also cited the April 8, 2026 ruling in Tolentino v. Heydarian, which emphasized that public discussions on matters of significant public interest should remain free and that courts must be wary of using their contempt powers to suppress critical speech.

"I welcome the opportunity to demonstrate that my comments were fair, made in good faith, and did not impede, obstruct, or degrade the administration of justice, and are thus constitutionally protected," Panelo said.
According to him, he would formally respond to the show cause order within the prescribed period upon receiving it.
The Senate impeachment court on Friday issued the show cause order against Panelo over his comments regarding the alleged partiality of several senator-judges. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: Vape users hospitalised after losing consciousness, prompting public health warning in New South Wales
articles.summary:
NSW health issues public warning about vape liquids containing etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas

Three people who lost consciousness and…

blocks.text: Three people who lost consciousness and were hospitalised in New South Wales after using certain vapes have tested positive for the unregulated anaesthetic agent etomidate, health officials have said.

NSW health on Friday issued a public warning about vape liquids containing etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for medical use in Australia.
The three people who were hospitalised had used non-nicotine refillable vapes, the state health department said. Testing of their blood and urine confirmed the presence of etomidate.
The department would not confirm how old the three patients were, where they were hospitalised, or their condition on Friday.
The discovery of etomidate in vapes in NSW comes about four months after Victorian health officials announced they had found the powerful anaesthetic agent in an illicit vape sold in Melbourne.
On Friday, NSW health warned vapes sold as space pods, space oil, kpods, piu piu vapes, or zombie vapes may contain etomidate, or other substances, including ketamine, THC and potent opioids.
The medical director of the NSW poisons information centre, Dr Darren Roberts, said etomidate’s effects were unpredictable when used in a vape.
Roberts said etomidate could cause confusion, drowsiness, slow breathing, vomiting, muscle spasms or movements that were hard to control, and people who took it could become unresponsive.
These effects could be life threatening, especially if used with other drugs that could cause sedation, such as alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, and GHB, Roberts said.
He said etomidate could also cause long term harm when used regularly, including the disruption of hormones produced by the adrenal gland.
These hormones are important in regulating stress responses and need to be replaced if they aren’t produced naturally, he said.
“The contents found in non-nicotine vapes vary,” Roberts said. “You can’t assume what’s inside.”
He urged anyone considering using a vape to ask themselves what could be in it.
“You won’t get into trouble for seeking medical care,” he said. If you feel unwell, or if your friend feels unwell, after using a vape, do something about it.”
NSW health officials said it recommended people administer Naloxone to anyone who became responsive after using any drug, in case they had ingested opioids.
Naloxone is an opioid overdose treatment, which is free at pharmacies and does not require a prescription.
Naloxone won’t reverse the effects of etomidate, as the sedative does not belong to the opioid class of drugs, but it is still safe to give, health officials said.
The officials said anyone who witnessed someone experiencing unexpected symptoms after using drugs should call triple zero immediately or seek urgent medical attention.

articles.summary: Marcos believes China wants South China Sea COC too

SHENZHEN, China —President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday said that he "felt strongly" that China also wants the Code of Conduct (COC) on the South China Sea be finalized soon, just like all member-states of the ASEAN.
In a Kapihan with the media, Marcos said he is “highly encouraged by the attitude” that China showcases with regard to the COC negotiations.
“Everyone is supportive of it, everyone is enthusiastic of it. For that matter, all sides…all the ASEAN leadership would like a COC,” Marcos said.
“And I think, I feel it very strongly that China would also like to have a COC. And they say so,” he added.
EXPLAINER: What is the South China Sea Code of Conduct?
Marcos said it is now up to Singapore, the next chair of ASEAN, to facilitate the anticipated finalization of the COC.
“The ball of course is now in Singapore's court. But everyone, all the shareholders in this matter have recognized the progress that we made during ASEAN in the Philippines,” he said.
The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) earlier said that Southeast Asian nations and China have completed negotiations on 80% of the COC.
Timeline: Rift deepens between PH, China over South China Sea
The South China Sea, or the West Philippine Sea for areas within Manila's 200-km exclusive economic zone, has been a point of contention between Beijing and Manila for years. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Baby born with heart abnormalities ‘didn’t have a chance’ after non-medical free birth, NSW inquest hears
articles.summary:
Inquest into the deaths of four babies after free and home births hears routine checks and follow-up may have saved their lives

Four babies who died in New South Wales – three after free…

blocks.text: Four babies who died in New South Wales – three after free births and one after a home birth – might have survived if they had had routine checks and follow-up , a coronial inquest has heard.
Baby DH, Baby D, Baby R, and Baby B died in the state’s northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024.
The inquest in Lismore has heard women chose free or home births for reasons including traumatic experiences, a lack of trust in clinicians, and a lack of services.

Baby DH died about eight hours after he was born in a free birth – with a doula but no medical professionals present. The court earlier heard he turned purple, was struggling to breathe and had became floppy.
His parents gave evidence they were worried but the doula kept reassuring them their baby was OK, then left.
The doula denied many of their claims, and denied that she gave them any clinical advice.

Expert neonatologist, associate professor Nicholas Evans, said on Friday Baby DH’s complex heart abnormalities “would have been readily detectable” in a routine pregnancy scan after which he would have been referred to a paediatric cardiologist.
It was a “missed opportunity”, he told the court.
Paediatric cardiologist Dr Paul Brooks said it was “highly likely” all the abnormalities would have been identified in a routine scan before birth.
Even if the extent of the abnormalities wasn’t clear, he told the court, the scan would have shown the baby needed to be born at a major hospital with cardiac surgery capabilities.
“The site of [Baby DH’s] birth meant that he didn’t have a chance.”
Baby D’s mother did not know she was having twins, and at first thought she’d delivered Baby D’s placenta, only to realise it was a stillborn second twin.

Experts at the inquest agreed it was impossible to know exactly why Baby D died. They discussed the possibility it was because self-described birth keeper Sita Tara Kali did not clamp the umbilical cord before cutting it, but ultimately, Evans told the court, it was most likely from respiratory distress because of his compromised heart function.

Baby D might have survived if someone who could do advanced resuscitation arrived in under 10 minutes, he said, but the “root cause” was that it was not known the mother was carrying twins before the births.
“If [twins] had been diagnosed, at 18 weeks, as it would usually in pregnancy, there would have been very close monitoring.”

Baby R likely died of “severe post-maturity” after being born at 43 weeks and one day in a free birth. The standard is to induce birth or perform a caesarean section at 42 weeks, as the ageing placenta puts the baby at risk.
The mother had been for an ultrasound at 12 weeks, which had put the date of birth at 28 July, 2020.
But the mother distrusted hospitals and trusted Kali, her birth keeper, the court previously heard.
Kali told her to calculate her due date from the date of conception, an unreliable measure that put the date of birth in mid August.
That recalculation, Evans wrote in his report to the court, was the “root cause” of the issue.
“The standard practice now is that you don’t allow a pregnancy to go beyond 42 completed weeks,” Evans said on Friday.
Expert midwives earlier told the court they don’t have statistics for babies born beyond 43 weeks, because it’s so rare.

A 19 August ultrasound showed the pregnancy had become a medical emergency – but Kali advised her to “go home and rest”. It is “more likely than not” that the baby would have survived had she gone to hospital after the ultrasound, Evans said.

Baby B’s mother was warned multiple times that she needed to go to hospital to give birth to her twins, but she was determined to have a home birth. Rather than let her have a free birth, four midwives assisted her and the head midwife repeatedly counselled her about the risks.
The mother declined ultrasounds as well as a test for early onset group B streptococcus (GBS) – an organism present in 15 to 20% of women that infects the babies of about 2% of carriers.
Baby B likely died of GBS, pneumonia and sepsis, Evans told the court on Friday, while his twin fell ill but survived. Many infected babies survive in hospital thanks to antibiotics, he added.
The inquest is ongoing.

Finance Minister Lars ​Klingbeil will begin the dialogue process on December ​2, when he welcomes economists from around the world to Berlin.

articles.title: AFP opens 2026 DAGITPA exercise with external defense focus
articles.summary: The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Friday opened the 10th iteration of its Dagat, Langit at Lupa (DAGITPA) exercise, with a focus on strengthening the country's external defense and…

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 2:38pm

The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Friday opened the 10th iteration of its Dagat, Langit at Lupa (DAGITPA) exercise, with a focus on strengthening the country's external defense and territorial integrity.

AFP chief General Antonio Nafarrete said the exercise aims to test the military's ability to conduct joint operations under realistic conditions, bringing together the capabilities of its different services.

"This security environment we face today requires an armed forces that can respond to threats to our sovereignty and territorial integrity," Nafarrete said during the opening ceremony at Camp Aguinaldo.

"This requires more than the capabilities of our individual services. We must be able to bring these capabilities together, make timely decisions, and carry out operations as one joint force," he added.
For Nafarrete, DAGITPA should be treated as a “mission rehearsal” rather than just another military exercise.

The exercise, known as AJEX DAGITPA 10-2026, is designed to enhance the AFP's ability to address current and emerging security challenges, particularly those involving territorial defense, maritime security, and cyber defense.

This exercise integrates the Philippine Army, Philippine Navy, Philippine Air Force, and Special Operations Forces to improve their capabilities in carrying out joint operations across land, sea, and air domains.

AJEX DAGITPA 10-2026 is scheduled from November 17 to 27, with major activities taking place within the joint operational areas of the Northern Luzon Command, Western Command, and National Capital Region Command.
The exercise has four major lines of effort: Command and Control Exercise, Field Training Exercise (FTX), Sustainment Exercise, and Humanitarian Civic Assistance.
FTX will cover three operational areas including Northern Luzon, West, and the National Capital Region.
Among the activities are integrated air and missile defense, air-sea battle, joint maritime strikes, maritime key terrain security operations, and counter-landing live-fire exercises.

For the defense of the West, the AFP will conduct operations focused on protecting sea lines of communication, securing offshore energy infrastructure, and testing anti-access and area denial capabilities.
Key areas include the Balabac Strait, Mindoro Strait, Pag-asa Island, and the offshore Nido Platform.

The exercise will also integrate cyber defense and information warfare scenarios to test the military's ability to respond to cyber-enabled threats and evolving disinformation campaigns. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Marcos 'perplexed' by Pax Silica rallies

SHENZHEN, China — President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday admitted he was puzzled by the massive protests staged across the country against the proposed Pax Silica initiative.
Speaking before reporters here, Marcos stressed that there are no specific provisions yet regarding the Pax Silica as there was nothing signed yet.
“I’m a little bit perplexed by the demonstrations in the Pax Silica because number one, there’s no deal yet,” Marcos said.
“If they are demonstrating against specific provisions, I don’t see that’s possible, there are no specific provisions. We haven’t done it yet,” he added.
During US President Donald Trump's visit to the Philippines early this week, both Marcos and US Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton said there was no signing of the initiative yet.
"There'll be no signing," Lipton said.
"No, not on this trip. We are not doing it. We are not covering that on this trip," Marcos said.

Announced in April, the Pax Silica initiative is a US-led effort to build a network of allied supply chains for critical technologies and minerals, which the Philippines will host in New Clark City in Tarlac.

articles.title: Nigeria moves to end jail terms for attempted suicide
articles.summary: Nigeria's proposed reform follows years of calls from psychiatrists and a parallel Senate bill.

blocks.text: Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has asked parliament to decriminalise attempted suicide, proposing medical support instead of prosecution for those who survive.
The proposal seeks to shift Nigeria's approach from criminal punishment to treatment and rehabilitation.
It follows years of calls for reform from mental health professionals. A separate bill seeking to decriminalise attempted suicide has already passed its second reading in the Senate.
Under Nigeria's law, attempted suicide is a criminal offence with those convicted facing up to one year's imprisonment, a fine or both.
The Senate bill also seeks to replace criminal penalties for attempted suicide with medical treatment, rehabilitation and support.
It was sponsored by Senator Asuquo Ekpenyong, who has argued that prosecuting people who survive suicide attempts could discourage those experiencing suicidal thoughts from seeking help.
He also warned that families might conceal such incidents for fear of prosecution and social stigma.
He stressed that the bill is not aimed at legalising or encouraging suicide attempts but rather protecting the survivors.
Tinubu's proposal has been welcomed by Senate President Godswill Akpabio, who had previously suggested that people who survived suicide attempts should be sent to prison.
"We are saying that suicide is a crime for now. Therefore, if you attempt it, we will send you to prison," Akpabio had said.
However, after receiving the Tinubu's proposal, he sought to clarify his earlier remarks, saying they did not apply to people experiencing mental health conditions.
He added that punishing people whose actions were influenced by mental health conditions would be insensitive.
Tinubu's letter follows sustained calls from mental health professionals for the law to be changed.

At a parliamentary public hearing in May 2024, the then president of the Association of Psychiatrists of Nigeria, Professor Taiwo Obindo, urged lawmakers to remove criminal penalties for attempted suicide.
"Why do we, as a nation, then punish individuals who are ill and need medical attention rather than prosecution?" he asked.
Drawing on his experience as a psychiatrist, Obindo said most people who die by suicide have a history of mental illness.
Akpabio has referred the president's amendment bill to the relevant senate committee for further consideration.
Nigeria is among several African countries where attempted suicide remains a criminal offence.
Ghana decriminalised attempted suicide in 2023, while Kenya's High Court ruled in January 2025 that the law criminalising it was unconstitutional.
If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.

articles.title: Fact check: Facebook reel twists survey findings on Sara Duterte impeachment
articles.summary: Facebook page Facts PH misrepresents Momentum Research survey figures to falsely claim most Filipinos believe Sara Duterte is guilty.

blocks.text: November 20, 2026 | 2:22pm
A Facebook reel misrepresents Momentum Research’s survey findings on public opinion of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment.
Facts PH / Screenshot
MANILA, Philippines — A Facebook reel misrepresents the findings of a public opinion research firm on the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Facebook page Facts PH shared a reel misrepresenting Momentum Research’s survey findings on Sara Duterte’s impeachment.
Screenshot taken Nov. 20, 2026, 1:40 p.m.
In a November 18 reel, Facebook page Facts PH attributed supposed findings to Momentum Research’s “latest” survey on whether Duterte is “guilty” or “innocent.”
The reel claimed that 64% of participants believed the vice president is guilty, while 23% allegedly said she is innocent.
Support for the prosecution also allegedly jumped from 26% to 38%, while support for the defense dropped to 17%, it added.
The post’s caption read:
Is public confidence in Sara Duterte’s defense fading? A new Momentum Research study reveals a growing divide: 64% of participants believe Duterte is guilty, while only 23% believe she is innocent.
Rating: This is false.
Facts
Momentum Research did not release any study stating 64% of participants believe the vice president is “guilty,” contrary to what the Facebook reel says.
Momentum Research’s October survey found varying levels of public acceptance for possible conviction or acquittal verdicts in Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial.

In its November 10 Facebook post, the firm published its October findings on public acceptance of potential impeachment court verdicts. The survey found that 32% would only accept the decision if it is to convict Duterte, 24% would only accept an acquittal, while 27% would accept either verdict.
Momentum Research’s October survey found that 38.8% of Filipino adults believe Sara Duterte should be convicted, while 33.8% believe she should be acquitted.
Momentum Research / Website
Meanwhile, 38.8% of Filipino adults believe Duterte should be convicted, while 33.8% believe she should be acquitted, according to its October 2026 National Momentum Survey.

There are no 64% or 23% figures in Momentum Research's published findings on whether Sara Duterte is considered “guilty” or “innocent.” The firm also makes no mention of these specific figures in relation to public opinion on the possible verdicts of the impeachment court.
Momentum Research’s August survey found that 64% of respondents agree or strongly agree that Duterte should return the P73 million in confidential funds disallowed by the Commission on Audit.
The figures cited in the Facebook reel appear to have been taken from the firm’s August 2026 survey on whether the vice president should return the Commission on Audit-disallowed confidential funds.
In the firm’s study, 64% agree or strongly agree that Duterte should return the P73 million in confidential funds, while 24% disagree or strongly disagree.
The same survey found that 23.3% of respondents believe Duterte’s defense team is outperforming the prosecution, while 15.2% say the prosecution is doing a better job.
Momentum Research / Facebook
In the same August survey, 23.3% believe Duterte's defense team is outperforming the prosecution, while 15.2% see the prosecution doing a better job.
These findings do not support the reel’s claim that the prosecution was gaining more support than the defense.
Why we fact-checked this
Friday, November 20, marks the 45th day of the vice president's impeachment proceedings, with the defense presenting more witnesses.
The impeachment trial currently centers on Article II of the Articles of Impeachment, concerning alleged unexplained wealth and failure to properly declare assets.
As of November 20, the Facebook reel has garnered more than 2,200 views and 30 reactions.
